chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: Project title: The 2025 Paradox: What Kazhydromet’s Data Leaves Out
Prepared by: Private Foundation “Almaty Air Initiative” Publication format: Electronic version, PDF
Publication date: March 2026 Almaty Air Initiative www.air.org.kz email: pa@air.org.kz Instagram: @air.org.kz

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 3 The Almaty Air Initiative foundation analyzed Kazhydromet’s official reports and publicly available raw data from its automated air quality monitoring stations for 2025. The analysis shows that air quality trends in Almaty in 2025 were contradictory.

Key Findings from the Annual Report The annual average pollution level decreased by 31%: The Air Pollution Index (API) fell from 5.8 to 4.0, formally placing the city in the “low pollution” category. Extreme pollution episodes became more severe: The Standard Index (SI) rose from 7.9 to 9.6 (+21.5%).

This means that, during a single episode, the maximum one-time concentration of a pollutant exceeded the maximum permissible concentration by approximately ten times. The annual Maximum Frequency Index increased: The Maximum Frequency Index (MFI) rose from 21% to 28% (+7 percentage points).

The number of exceedances of maximum permissible concentrations (MPCs) changed substantially: Exceedances of the maximum one-time MPC for ozone fell approximately 100-fold (−99%), while exceedances for nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) increased to 12,309 (+11.6%), and for nitric oxide (NO) to 2,749 (+50.2%).

Annual average citywide concentrations calculated from the raw data of automated stations, excluding manual monitoring posts, were*: PM2.5: 14.27 µg/m³ PM10: 23.7 µg/m³ SO₂: 25.0 µg/m³ CO: 484.4 µg/m³ NO₂: 39.8 µg/m³ NO: 32.7 µg/m³ O₃: 4.

9 µg/m³ Differences between stations reach several orders of magnitude: According to automated monitoring stations, annual average PM2.5 concentrations at individual locations range from less than 1 µg/m³ to 43.6 µg/m³, warranting close examination of the monitoring network’s structure.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 4 The year was warmer and substantially drier than 2024: In some months, precipitation was several times below normal, and weather conditions were often dominated by anticyclones with light winds. These conditions restrict the mixing of air masses and reduce natural atmospheric cleansing, contributing to pollutant accumulation near the ground.

The 2025 Paradox: Lower Background Levels, Higher Peaks According to official data, Almaty’s air became “cleaner” in 2025 (Figure 1). A closer examination, however, reveals a more complex picture. Figure 1. Comparison of the Standard Index (SI), Maximum Frequency Index (MFI), and Air Pollution Index (API) in Almaty, 2021–2025.

Source: “Information Bulletin on the State of the Environment in Almaty City, Almaty Region and Zhetysu Region, 2025” To assess overall background pollution, Kazhydromet uses the Air Pollution Index (API).

Additional indicators are used to provide a more complete picture: SI (Standard Index) reflects the most severe pollution episode and shows how many times the maximum concentration exceeded the established limit. MFI (Maximum Frequency Index) shows how often pollutant concentrations exceeded permissible levels.

The report uses the MFI for a single monitoring post. According to the agency’s annual report, average background pollution in Almaty declined by 31% in 2025 (API: 5.8 → 4.1) compared with 2024, formally corresponding to the “low pollution” category on the API scale.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 5 The report also records marked declines in several indicators. The number of registered exceedances of the maximum one-time permissible concentration (MPC) for ozone dropped by 99% (from 8,036 to 77 episodes); for carbon monoxide (CO), by 79.6% (from 4,406 to 898); for PM2.

5, by 34% (from 3,236 to 2,131); for PM10, by 29% (from 1,091 to 772); and for sulfur dioxide, by 25% (from 2,271 to 1,704). For reference: API (Air Pollution Index) – an indicator reflecting annual average pollution levels across a group of priority pollutants.

SI (Standard Index) – an indicator reflecting the most extreme one-time pollutant concentration recorded during the year. MFI (Maximum Frequency Index) – an indicator describing how frequently concentrations exceed sanitary standards at one monitoring post. At first glance, these figures suggest an overall improvement in air quality.

However, the composition of pollution changed noticeably. While ozone was among the leading pollutants in terms of exceedances in 2024 (8,036 cases), its contribution almost disappeared in 2025 (77 cases). At the same time, nitrogen compounds became more prominent (Table 1): nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) exceedances rose from 11,024 to 12,309 (+11.
6%), while nitric oxide (NO) exceedances increased from 1,830 to 2,749 (+50.2%). Comparing these figures with the raw data, however, reveals certain discrepancies.

Such substantial changes may be associated not only with actual changes in air quality but also with measurement practices, including the number of readings and data processing methods.

What the Raw Data from Automated Monitoring Stations Reveal To understand how the annual report’s final indicators are produced, it is important to examine the measurements on which they are based. In addition to the aggregated data in Kazhydromet’s annual report, we

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 7 conducted an independent analysis of raw ambient air quality measurements for 2025. Kazhydromet provided the data in response to an official request. According to Kazhydromet, Almaty has 16 air quality monitoring posts. Twelve are automated stations that take continuous measurements every 20 minutes.
All stations undergo annual verification and are officially certified as measuring instruments. The remaining four posts use manual sampling, with measurements taken three times daily.
This analysis considers only data from automated stations, since they provide continuous measurement time series that make it possible to assess air pollution trends throughout the year.

To determine how completely automated monitoring stations capture concentrations of different pollutants and how measurements are spatially distributed across the city, we developed a coverage map of automated air quality monitoring stations (Figure 2).

Each point represents a monitoring station and is labeled with its identifier, allowing readers to compare its geographic location with the statistical indicators presented in the table. To the left of the map, a summary table presents key statistical characteristics of the pollutant concentrations measured at the stations during 2025.

For each pollutant (PM2.5, PM10, SO₂, CO, NO₂, NO and O₃), it provides: the annual average concentration; data coverage (the percentage of time during which the station transmitted valid measurements); the minimum and maximum recorded values.

The table uses color coding to indicate data completeness: Green – stable, sufficient coverage (≥80% of days with valid data); Yellow – moderate data completeness (≥50%); Red – low completeness (<50%); Gray – no measurements or unavailable data for the relevant pollutant.
The map therefore illustrates the actual basis of the calculations: which monitoring locations contribute to the city’s “average air” and how representative the resulting values are.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 8 Figure 2. Coverage map of Kazhydromet’s automated air quality monitoring stations and pollution statistics (link to the detailed interactive map) Important Considerations Incomplete range of measured pollutants: Not all automated stations have analyzers for every pollutant, so measurements for particular substances may be entirely absent from seasonal charts throughout the year.
Even where the official report lists a broad range of monitored pollutants, the dataset actually provided contains no measurements for certain substances at some stations. For example, PM2.

5 and PM10 data are completely missing for Skat-2, Skat-5 and Station 27; SO₂ data are missing for Skat-4; and O₃ data are missing for Station 29, despite these pollutants appearing in the report’s list of monitored substances. Consequently, citywide annual average estimates for individual

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 9 pollutants are based on a limited number of monitoring locations rather than the entire network. Differences in data completeness: Some stations provide almost continuous measurements (more than 98–100% of days with valid data), while others exhibit significant gaps.

These may be associated with equipment maintenance, instrument calibration, interruptions in data transmission or the operating characteristics of particular analyzers. As a result, individual stations may contribute differently to final citywide indicators depending on the pollutant.

Zero values in annual data require cautious interpretation: In some cases, annual average concentrations at individual stations are displayed as 0.00 µg/m³ (for example, NO₂ and NO at Station 27), sometimes over long periods.

In a major city, such concentrations are virtually never encountered in practice: even very clean air contains background aerosols and gases. As a rule, these values suggest an absence of recorded measurements rather than an absence of pollution, for example because of prolonged equipment downtime or data export procedures.

Anomalous data discretization and sensitivity thresholds (the Skat-2 case): Examination of the raw data reveals technical anomalies that raise doubts about how accurately certain stations reflect actual environmental conditions. A striking example is the nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) data from Skat-2.
The dataset exhibits unnatural discretization: readings “jump” between 0 and 100 µg/m³, while numerous values above 200 µg/m³ appear, at which point variability resumes.

This distribution may indicate a software or hardware limitation (a lower detection threshold) whereby the instrument ignores real fluctuations in concentrations at the lower end of the range. Geographic distortion of indicators (the Skat-2 case): Automated station Skat-2 is located outside Almaty’s administrative boundaries.
Including its readings in citywide calculations distorts actual pollution indicators because it measures a suburban background that may differ from smog concentrations in urban neighborhoods.

On the one hand, air pollution does not respect administrative boundaries, and the transport of pollutants between the city and its suburbs is a natural process. On the other hand, including a suburban station may affect the final citywide figures, particularly if pollution at that site differs severalfold from levels within the city.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: Why the City May Look Cleaner (or Dirtier) on Paper To assess the consistency of the results, we compared indicators calculated from the raw data of 12 automated stations, covering only seven main pollutants (PM2.5, PM10, SO₂, CO, NO₂, NO and O₃), with the aggregated figures in Kazhydromet’s official 2025 annual report.

Differences between calculated and official values may therefore arise from differences in the stations included, the inclusion of manual monitoring posts in official statistics, data processing procedures and other factors. The most notable differences are: PM10: The difference in exceedance counts (+116 cases) may reflect data aggregation procedures and differences in the stations used. NO, CO and PM2.5: There are some discrepancies in the number of maximum one-time MPC exceedances, but annual average indicators are virtually identical.

Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), especially at Skat-2, which lies beyond Almaty’s administrative boundary, deserves particular attention. The greatest difference concerns the number of exceedances (Table 3). When Skat-2 is included, the calculated number of exceedances (12,118) is very close to the official figure (12,309).
When it is excluded, however, the number falls to 4,817 — 7,492 fewer than in the official statistics. This indicates the substantial influence of one station on the final citywide indicator.

−17 0.01 0.01 1.03 1.03 Maximum one-time concentrations, meanwhile, match almost completely, supporting the accuracy of how extreme values were processed. An analysis of raw data from individual monitoring stations reveals technical anomalies that call into question whether they accurately reflect actual environmental conditions.

The operation of Skat-2 when measuring nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is a particularly striking example. Its dataset shows unnatural discretization: values “jump” between 0 and 100 µg/m³, while many readings exceed 200 µg/m³, above which variability resumes.

This pattern suggests a possible software or hardware limitation (a lower reporting threshold) that causes the instrument to ignore real concentration fluctuations in the lower range. Figure 3 illustrates the 2025 time series of NO₂ readings at Skat-2.
According to Kazhydromet’s 2025 report, readings from Skat-2 were responsible for the high Maximum Frequency Index (MFI = 28%) recorded for the city.

Examination of the visualization suggests that the elevated concentrations reported by Kazhydromet in 2025 may be attributable less to actual environmental conditions than to how measuring instruments operate or record data.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 13 Figure 3. Hourly average nitrogen dioxide readings from Automated Monitoring Post No. 2 (Skat-2), Turksib District, Burunday Motor Depot, Aerodromnaya Street (link to the interactive chart) A similar situation is observed for nitric oxide at Automated Station No. 5.

Kazhydromet classified air pollution in Almaty in 2025 as high according to the Standard Index (SI = 9.6), based on a nitric oxide (NO) concentration of 1,960 µg/m³ recorded at Station No. 5 near Halyk Arena. Changes in the station’s nitric oxide readings are presented in Figure 4.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 14 Figure 4. Hourly average nitric oxide readings from Automated Monitoring Post No. 5 (Skat-5), Medeu District, Halyk Arena ice rink, Duman Microdistrict (link to the interactive chart) At Station No. 5, concentrations remained stable at approximately 7–9 µg/m³ for most of the year until October 14.

There was then a noticeable step change, with readings stabilizing at 22 µg/m³. Between December 16 and 24, sharp spikes reached 2,963 µg/m³, after which concentrations returned to approximately 22 µg/m³ through the end of the year (Figure 4).

This pattern is inconsistent with nitrogen oxide measurements described in the scientific literature and with data from independent sensors in 2023–2024, as documented in an Almaty Air Initiative report. It may also reflect the operating or data-recording characteristics of the instruments.

These data “anomalies” suggest that the city’s official designation as having “low pollution” may, in some cases, be based on incorrect instrument operation or data recording. The analysis shows that Skat-2 and Skat-5 are not isolated cases.

Examination of 2025 time series from other monitoring posts, including stations in other regions of Kazakhstan, indicates that critically high (or low) values influencing final city pollution indices are often attributable not to natural or human-caused environmental factors but entirely to hardware or software behavior.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 15 Trends in PM2.5 Particulate Matter Readings Although PM2.5 concentrations display clear seasonal changes in the chart of daily average values for 2025, the datasets from some stations contain characteristics that warrant further analysis. Figure 5. Daily average PM2.

5 readings from Kazhydromet’s automated monitoring stations (link to the interactive chart) The daily average concentration chart shows the typical annual pattern of air pollution in Almaty (Figure 5): winter months (January–February) are characterized by high concentrations associated with the heating season and unfavorable meteorological conditions; pollution levels decline noticeably during spring and summer as atmospheric circulation becomes stronger; concentrations begin to rise again in autumn and early winter.

For example, Station 28 recorded extreme daily average values exceeding 250 µg/m³ in January, consistent with severe urban smog episodes also observed by independent sensor networks. Overall, this pattern corresponds to the established seasonal structure of air pollution in Almaty.
A closer look at the chart, however, shows that not all stations exhibit comparable concentration variability.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 16 Against the pronounced seasonal changes observed at several stations, almost horizontal lines stand out in some time series, particularly those for Skat-3 and Skat-4. For much of the year, their readings remain close to zero or almost unchanged, while neighboring stations record noticeable fluctuations. This pattern is unusual for urban air.

Under real-world conditions, even when air is relatively clean, PM2.5 concentrations: respond to weather changes; vary during peaks in economic activity; increase during temperature inversions; exhibit clear seasonality.

Prolonged periods of nearly identical readings may therefore indicate not exceptionally clean air but characteristics of the instruments’ operation or data recording. This inconsistency is also clearly visible in the chart of annual average PM2.
5 concentrations across Kazhydromet stations (Figure 6), where concentrations differ by an order of magnitude between sites.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 17 Figure 6. Average PM2.5 concentrations based on data from Kazhydromet’s automated monitoring stations Such a large variation within a single urban monitoring network is excessive. For comparison, according to the Almaty Air Initiative annual report, which is based on an independent sensor network, Almaty’s annual average PM2.

5 concentration in 2025 was 31.2 µg/m³. This value is close to readings from Skat-6 and Station 28 and significantly higher than those reported by most other stations in the national air quality monitoring network.

Skat-3 (near Almaty Arena) and Skat-4 (near the Ili Highway) are particularly striking: their annual average values are below 1 µg/m³ (!) If these readings alone were used as a reference, Almaty could be considered one of the cleanest cities in the world, since such concentrations are lower than those found in many remote natural areas.

In a major city where coal is used, traffic is heavy and road dust is common, annual PM2.5 concentrations below 1 µg/m³ appear atypical compared with other available data and may warrant additional technical verification. For comparison, according to IQAir’s 2024–2025 reports, even the cleanest places

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 18 on Earth have concentrations above 1 µg/m³. For instance, Mayagüez, Puerto Rico — an island city exposed to ocean winds — has an average concentration of 1.1 µg/m³ (IQAir cleanest cities ranking). Trends in Ground-Level Ozone (O₃) Concentrations Ground-level ozone (O₃) trends deserve separate attention (Figure 7).

According to Kazhydromet’s official report, the number of ozone standard exceedances fell by 99% in 2025 compared with 2024. At first glance, this could suggest that the problem of photochemical air pollution has almost disappeared.

However, analysis of daily average ozone concentrations shows that monitoring stations differ substantially not only in the levels they record but also in the patterns of change over time. Figure 7. Average ozone concentrations recorded by Automated Monitoring Posts No. 30, No.

31 and AQM1 (link to the interactive chart) Ozone is a secondary pollutant formed in the atmosphere through photochemical reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds under sunlight. It therefore typically exhibits a relatively consistent seasonal pattern: higher concentrations in summer; lower concentrations in winter.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 19 Yet the daily average concentration chart reveals substantial differences in ozone behavior between stations, including characteristics at certain sites that require cautious interpretation. 1. Station No. 30 — incomplete time series. Ozone data completeness at Station 30 is approximately 48%.

In practice, readings are available only for the first half of the year, mostly through June. A substantial proportion of observations during this period are recorded as zero. The time series is almost entirely missing in the second half of the year.

Consequently, this station’s data do not allow an assessment of the characteristic summer ozone peaks that normally occur during warmer months. 2. AQM1 — atypical seasonal pattern. This station shows unusual seasonality.
The chart indicates that ozone concentrations remain relatively low and stable during the first half of the year, followed by abrupt, short-lived peaks reaching much higher values in the second half.

This pattern differs from typical ozone seasonality, in which concentrations usually increase gradually as sunlight intensity and air temperatures rise. It may reflect several factors: the station’s location, nearby sources of ozone precursors, or technical characteristics of data recording. 3. Station No.

31 — abrupt change in concentrations during the year. The chart shows that ozone readings are almost entirely absent or remain at zero in the first half of the year. From approximately the second half onward, concentrations rise sharply and begin to show much higher values.
Why This Matters for the Citywide Average A city’s air quality indicator is usually calculated as an average across its monitoring station network.

If some stations report abnormally low or high concentrations, show long periods of identical readings, or have incomplete time series, the final annual average pollution estimate may be substantially distorted.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 20 In other words, averaging such data can produce citywide indicators that are considerably lower than the actual pollution levels recorded in the city’s most heavily affected areas. To understand how pollution changes throughout the year, monthly average pollutant concentrations were analyzed across automated monitoring stations (Figure 8).

Figure 8. Seasonal trends in monthly average pollutant concentrations recorded by Kazhydromet’s automated monitoring stations (Almaty, 2025) (link to the interactive chart) Seasonal trends for most pollutants follow the expected pattern (Figure 8): higher concentrations during colder months and lower concentrations during warmer periods.
However, for certain pollutants and monitoring stations, apparent drops or abrupt changes may be associated not with actual changes in air quality, but with the way data is collected and recorded.

As a result, seasonal charts for individual pollutants reflect not only actual changes in concentrations but also the structure and completeness of the available measurements. The monthly chart shows that, for several pollutants, the lines remain almost flat throughout the year.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 21 Under real-world conditions in a major city with our climate, such patterns are extremely rare. Pollutant concentrations typically vary significantly from month to month due to: temperature changes and the heating season; wind patterns; traffic intensity; photochemical processes in the atmosphere.

Therefore, prolonged flat sections on the charts may indicate several possible factors: extended periods of analyzer downtime; repeated reporting of identical values when no new measurements are available; data processing or export procedures; technical malfunctions at individual stations or calibration-related issues.

These characteristics call for cautious interpretation of annual indicators, as even a small number of stations reporting incorrect or identical values can noticeably affect the final citywide average.

Annual Average Pollutant Concentrations by District Annual average pollutant concentrations were calculated for each of the city’s administrative districts using data from 12 automated monitoring stations (Figure 9).

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 22 Figure 9. Annual average pollutant concentrations by Almaty district, based on data from Kazhydromet’s automated monitoring stations (2025) It is important to note that some districts have no automated monitoring stations, with observations conducted only at manual monitoring posts, whose data were not included in this analysis.

Therefore, the spatial analysis covers only districts for which automated monitoring station data are available. The highest concentrations of carbon monoxide (CO) were recorded in Alatau District, at approximately 710 µg/m³, and Medeu District, at around 714 µg/m³.
Concentrations in Bostandyk District and near the Burunday Motor Depot were approximately 537–526 µg/m³. The lowest CO concentrations were recorded in Turksib District, at around 181 µg/m³.

For nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), the highest concentrations were observed near the Burunday Motor Depot and in Zhetysu District, at approximately 92–94 µg/m³, while concentrations in Alatau and Medeu Districts were significantly lower, at around 17–22 µg/m³. Nitric oxide (NO) also shows substantial variation.

Its annual average concentration exceeds 120 µg/m³ near the Burunday Motor Depot and reaches approximately 42 µg/m³ in Zhetysu District, while in Bostandyk District it is close to 5 µg/m³. For particulate matter, the differences are less pronounced but consistent. Annual average PM2.5 concentrations range from 1.
4 µg/m³ in Alatau District to 17 µg/m³ in Turksib District and 32 µg/m³ in Zhetysu District. For PM10, the highest concentrations reach 39 µg/m³, while the lowest are approximately 1.5 µg/m³.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) concentrations in most districts range from 5 to 55 µg/m³, with elevated levels in Alatau and Zhetysu Districts. Annual average ozone (O₃) concentrations range from 3 to 5 µg/m³, showing relatively moderate spatial variation. A comparison of Kazhydromet’s PM2.
5 data with the Almaty Air Initiative (AAI) 2025 report reveals substantial discrepancies:
Comparison of PM2.5 Concentrations by District (µg/m³) District
Kazhydromet PM2.5 (automated stations) Turksib 17.0 Zhetysu 32.2
Alatau 1.4 Bostandyk 14.4 Almaty Air Initiative PM2.5 (AAI) 46.8 37.9 37.7 22.1

Difference 2.7 times comparable 27 times (!) 1.5 times While Kazhydromet reports a downward trend in average background pollution levels, AAI data indicate that pollution levels have remained high or even increased (by 30% compared with 2024).

Possible reasons for these discrepancies include differences in the density and structure of the monitoring networks, the stations included in the calculations, the accuracy of data recording, data completeness, and aggregation methods, all of which can affect the final annual average values differently.

Both sources confirm that Turksib District is among the areas experiencing elevated pollution levels. However, their estimates differ: 17.0 µg/m³ according to Kazhydromet versus 46.8 µg/m³ according to AAI.
The figure reported by Kazhydromet is comparable to pollution levels in several European capitals, whereas the AAI value reflects higher pollution levels recorded by a dense sensor network.

The difference may be explained by the density and placement of monitoring stations: the AAI network includes more measurement locations and is not limited to sites with more favorable air circulation conditions.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 24 The substantial discrepancy in Alatau District (1.4 versus 37.7 µg/m³) is likely associated with technical factors affecting government monitoring stations, such as periods of analyzer malfunction or calibration-related issues. A concentration of 1.4 µg/m³ appears exceptionally low for an urban district and requires additional verification.

For comparison, concentrations of around 1 µg/m³ are characteristic of remote, sparsely urbanized areas, such as oceanic islands. In Alatau District, where traffic, urban development, and solid-fuel heating are present, such a low concentration appears atypical. At the same time, the AAI figure of 37.
7 µg/m³ is consistent with pollution levels observed in major cities with complex terrain and a significant share of households using solid-fuel heating.

These findings highlight the importance of combined monitoring approaches: government monitoring stations provide certified data, while independent monitoring networks offer denser coverage across the city.

Distribution of Pollutant Concentrations (Based on Daily Values) Additionally, the distribution of daily average concentrations for each pollutant was analyzed using data from automated monitoring stations (Figure 10).

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 25 Figure 10. Distribution of daily average pollutant concentrations based on data from Kazhydromet’s automated monitoring stations (Almaty, 2025) Unlike average values, concentration distributions help explain how the final indicator is formed: whether it reflects a consistent background pollution level or rare but significant concentration peaks.

Key Observations PM2.5 and PM10: The distributions are strongly right-skewed: most days are characterized by moderate concentrations, but there are periods with substantially elevated values. For example, during winter, some stations recorded daily PM2.

5 concentrations exceeding 200–250 µg/m³, tens of times higher than World Health Organization guidelines. In other words, air quality may appear relatively “average” for much of the year, while several dozen days account for a substantial share of the city’s actual pollution burden.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 26 Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂): The distribution is wider, with a noticeable tail of high concentrations. This means that nitrogen dioxide exceedances do not occur only as isolated spikes but may persist for several consecutive days. Such distributions contribute to relatively high annual average concentrations in certain districts.

The Skat-2 station, located near the Burunday Motor Depot, plays a particularly significant role in the city’s pollution statistics. Analysis of the raw data shows that a substantial proportion of recorded NO₂ exceedances comes from this monitoring location.

This pattern requires cautious interpretation, as the significant contribution of a single station to citywide statistics may considerably influence the final air pollution assessment, particularly for nitrogen compounds.

Nitric oxide (NO): Several stations exhibit substantial variability, ranging from numerous days with low concentrations to occasional pronounced peaks. This reflects the indicator’s sensitivity to local conditions and short-term emission sources. Particular attention should be paid to the time series from Skat-5, located near Halyk Arena.
In 2025, this station recorded the maximum one-time nitric oxide concentration that determined the city’s Standard Index (SI = 9.6).

However, the station’s readings show a distinctive pattern throughout the year: concentrations remain relatively stable for an extended period, followed by an abrupt change in levels and the appearance of pronounced peaks.

Carbon monoxide (CO): The distributions show a shift toward elevated concentrations at certain stations, while readings on most days remain within a relatively stable range. This suggests a comparatively consistent background concentration with periodic increases.

Sulfur dioxide (SO₂): In most cases, the distribution is concentrated within a relatively narrow range, without pronounced extreme spikes, resulting in a smoother annual pattern. At the same time, the time series shows (Figure 10) that such peaks are episodic: after brief periods of elevated concentrations, readings return to low levels.

At most other stations across the city, SO₂ concentrations remain significantly lower and also exhibit more stable patterns throughout the year. Ozone (O₃): The distributions are compact, without significant extreme values, suggesting a more uniform pattern of ozone formation throughout the year. However, closer examination of the raw data

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 27 reveals substantial measurement gaps and inconsistencies in the time series at several stations. Some monitoring locations report prolonged periods of zero readings or incomplete time series, while others show abrupt changes in concentration levels during the year.
As a result, these distributions may reflect the availability and completeness of monitoring data rather than actual changes in atmospheric ozone concentrations.

The analysis of concentration distributions shows that differences between districts and monitoring stations are determined not only by average pollution levels but also by how concentrations vary throughout the year.

For certain pollutants, particularly nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter, annual indicators depend significantly on the number of days with elevated concentrations, whereas other pollutants exhibit a more uniform pattern.

Meteorological Conditions Meteorological conditions significantly influence the formation and dispersion of air pollutants. Temperature patterns, precipitation, wind conditions, and prevailing atmospheric circulation determine how intensely pollutants accumulate and how air pollution develops in urban environments.

The following section presents a comparative analysis of meteorological conditions in Almaty in 2024 and 2025, based on Kazhydromet’s annual reports. Precipitation In 2025, precipitation was significantly lower than in 2024, negatively affecting the atmosphere’s natural cleansing processes: February was predominantly dry.

In April 2025, precipitation was approximately half the normal amount (53.3 mm compared with the normal 112 mm), whereas April 2024 was close to the climatic norm (110 mm). During summer (June–August) 2025, precipitation was 2–20 times below normal (2.
3 mm in July), whereas in July 2024, precipitation was almost twice the normal amount (82 mm compared with the normal 43 mm).

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 28 Overall, 2025 was considerably drier than 2024 in certain months, particularly during spring and summer. Air Temperature In 2025, temperatures tended to be higher than in 2024, as confirmed by data for several key periods: April: Temperatures in 2025 were 3°C above normal, whereas in 2024 they remained within the climatic norm.

Summer: July 2025 was classified as “very hot,” with temperatures exceeding the norm, while July 2024 was close to normal. In August 2025, temperatures were 1°C above normal. By comparison, the first half of August 2024 was hot, but the second half was cooler, with daytime temperatures dropping to +21°C.
December: December 2025 was significantly warmer, with the monthly average temperature 3.6°C above normal. In contrast, December 2024 was 1°C below normal.

Atmospheric Pressure Patterns and Anticyclone Influence A key distinguishing feature of 2025 was increased anticyclonic activity, which directly contributes to stagnant air conditions and smog accumulation. February 2025: Unlike the unstable weather conditions of February 2024, Almaty was frequently influenced by an anticyclone in 2025.

This resulted in predominantly dry weather and a 20.4 mm reduction in precipitation (2.2 times less than in 2024). November 2025: Periods of anticyclonic conditions were recorded, accompanied by nighttime temperatures falling to −2°C to −7°C amid an overall precipitation deficit (26.4 mm less than in November 2024).
Atmospheric stability: Weather conditions in June and July 2025 were characterized as “stable.” Under prevailing anticyclonic conditions, this limits the vertical mixing of air masses.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 29 Wind Conditions Wind activity, which helps ventilate the city, remained predominantly low in both years. However, several differences were observed: In May 2024, wind gusts reached 18 m/s, whereas in May 2025, the maximum wind speed did not exceed 9 m/s (a twofold decrease in intensity).

In June and July 2025, maximum wind speeds were slightly higher (up to 16–17 m/s) than in 2024 (up to 6–15 m/s). During winter and autumn months (January, February, September, and October), light winds prevailed in both years, with speeds generally not exceeding 4–9 m/s.

These conditions contribute to the accumulation of harmful pollutants in the near-surface atmospheric layer. Summary Compared with 2024, 2025 was characterized by: Higher temperatures, particularly during spring and summer and toward the end of the year.

A significant precipitation deficit during most months (particularly in spring and midsummer, when precipitation was 2–35 times lower), reducing the removal of pollutants from the atmosphere through precipitation.
Persistently low wind speeds, which, combined with the precipitation deficit in 2025, created less favorable conditions for pollutant dispersion than in 2024.

Main Sources of Air Pollution (Almaty and Almaty Region) According to Kazhydromet’s annual report, the regional emissions situation remains challenging, while traffic-related pressure continues to increase. 1. Stationary emission sources.
According to the statistics presented in the report, the region had a total of 8,974 stationary emission sources in 2025, including:

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 30 organized emission sources — 5,581; sources equipped with emission control systems — 1,078. This means that approximately 88% of facilities are not equipped with emission control systems.

However, the document does not provide an estimate of the total pollution generated by these facilities, making it difficult to assess their actual contribution to overall air pollution levels. 2. Private houses.

According to data from Almaty’s Green Economy Department cited in the report, the city had a total of 151,059 private houses in 2025, including: houses using gas heating — 149,341. The report also states that the gasification rate of residential houses is 98.8%.
However, this calculation may not fully account for buildings in informal development areas, temporary structures, and private bathhouses, where coal or other fuels may be used for heating.

Furthermore, the analysis provides only limited consideration of the Almaty metropolitan area, from which air currents may transport emissions from suburban settlements into the city’s basin. 3. Motor vehicles.
According to Almaty Police Department data cited by Kazhydromet, a total of 643,470 motor vehicles were registered, representing an increase of 12,745 vehicles compared with 2024.

These included: passenger cars — 578,022 (33,955 more than the previous year); buses — 11,208 (862 more than in 2024); trucks — 43,648 (2,746 more than in 2024); special-purpose vehicles — 1,258 (89 more than in 2024); motorcycles and other motorized two-wheelers — 9,334 (1,014 more than in 2024).

The report also notes an increase in the vehicle fleet compared with the previous year, amounting to 41,734 vehicles in 2025. At the same time, the number of exceedances increased for nitric oxide (+50.2%) and nitrogen dioxide (+11.6%). The report does not provide an

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 31 assessment of the contribution of each emission source to overall pollution levels. Conclusions An analysis of official air quality monitoring data and raw measurements shows that the air quality situation in Almaty in 2025 presents a mixed picture.
Formally, several indicators suggest improvement: the average pollution level decreased according to official statistics, and the Air Pollution Index moved into the “low pollution” category.

However, a more detailed analysis of time series, concentration distributions, and the structure of the monitoring network reveals systemic problems in the national air quality monitoring network in Almaty. First, average indicators may depend significantly on the structure of the monitoring network and data completeness.

Several stations report prolonged periods of identical or zero readings, while data for certain pollutants are missing or available only as incomplete time series. Under these conditions, a decline in citywide pollution indicators may reflect not only improvements in air quality but also the characteristics of the measurement process.

In other words, the city may appear to be “getting cleaner” in official statistics faster than it actually is. Second, the composition of air pollution has changed. Despite declines in several indicators, the number of nitrogen dioxide exceedances remains very high, pointing to the growing influence of transport.

At the same time, a substantial proportion of these exceedances comes from a single monitoring station (Skat-2) located outside the city’s administrative boundaries. This raises further questions about how the final citywide pollution assessment is calculated.

Third, meteorological conditions in 2025 were themselves unfavorable for pollutant dispersion. Warmer weather, insufficient precipitation, frequent anticyclones, and weak winds created conditions in which pollutants remained in the near-surface atmospheric layer for longer periods.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: what Kazhydromet's data leaves out
blocks: 32 Another important aspect, often overlooked in public discussions, must also be considered. Decisions to classify pollution levels as high and, in particular, to declare periods of adverse meteorological conditions (AMC), are based not only on regulatory standards but also on actual monitoring data.

If the monitoring system has data gaps, is sensitive to technical limitations, or fails to capture certain concentration fluctuations, some pollution episodes may simply be absent from the official picture. As a result, the city may appear to have “better” air quality on dashboards than what people actually experience at street level.

This does not necessarily indicate a problem with the regulatory standards themselves. Rather, it highlights that the accuracy of air quality assessments directly depends on the quality and completeness of measurements.
The main conclusion is straightforward: average indicators may create an impression of improvement, but they do not always reflect the actual environmental burden on the city.

To assess air quality objectively, it is important to consider not only the final figures but also how they are produced: which monitoring stations are included in the calculations, how accurate and complete the data are, and which pollution episodes fall outside the averages.

In this context, improving the monitoring system itself — increasing data completeness, ensuring the comparability of measurements, and making methodologies more transparent — is just as important as discussing regulatory standards. Ultimately, this determines how accurately the city can “see” the air its residents breathe.

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: Summary This report presents the findings of the third annual study of public
perceptions of air quality in Almaty. The study was prepared by the
Almaty Air Initiative Foundation in collaboration with political scientist
Serik Beissembayev. At the Foundation’s request, PwC Kazakhstan reviewed the report on a

pro bono basis and provided its expert opinion. The purpose of the study is to assess residents’ levels of awareness, willingness to act, and actual behavior in relation to air pollution, and to track changes compared with the 2024 and 2025 survey waves.

The Index is designed as a management tool: a reproducible annual indicator that can be used to assess the effectiveness of the city’s environmental and information policies and to compare Almaty with other cities.
For the first time in the current sociological study, the Air Quality Awareness Index was calculated as a composite indicator that brings survey results onto a common scale from 0 to 100.

The Index assumes that awareness is not limited to knowledge but consists of a sequence of four stages. Residents first perceive air pollution as a threat, then learn about its causes and ways to check air quality, then develop a willingness to act, and

only after that translate this willingness into actual behavior. Each stage is measured separately, allowing the Index to show not only the overall level of awareness, but also the specific point at which the chain may break down. A higher Index score indicates a more comprehensive understanding of the problem and more active behavior.

The fieldwork was conducted from 18 February to 11 March 2026. Total of 1,000 Almaty residents aged 18 and above were surveyed. The sample is representative of the city’s adult population by gender, age, and district of residence and covers all eight administrative districts. The statistical margin of error does not exceed ±3.1 percentage points.

The Index methodology is based on the approaches set out in the Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (OECD / Joint Research Centre of the European Commission). The overall Index score for Almaty is 41 out of 100, corresponding to the category “low level, predominantly passive attitude.”

Behind this figure lies a stable pattern that constitutes the central finding of the study. Air pollution is recognized as a problem almost universally across the city: the overwhelming majority of residents consider air pollution dangerous to health, and this proportion has increased for the third

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: consecutive year. However, knowledge of where to check air quality and what measures are
implemented remains limited to a minority of residents. Willingness to
act declines noticeably as soon as a measure affects residents’ own
everyday behavior. Actual practices are the least widespread, and they are
dominated by strategies of personal protection and avoidance rather than

participation. In other words, concern about air pollution is high, while the knowledge and practical experience required to translate this concern into action remain insufficient. The gap between emotional perception of the problem and practical behavior is the most

pronounced characteristic of the overall profile, and data from the three survey waves indicate that it has not yet narrowed. One finding that extends beyond the environmental agenda deserves particular attention.

The proportion of residents seriously considering moving away from Almaty has increased noticeably over the past two years, and most of them cite air quality as the main reason. At the same time, this intention remains reversible: half of potential movers would abandon their plans to relocate if the situation improved significantly.
Air quality is therefore identified by the study not only as an environmental factor, but also as a demographic one.
Methodology The study is based on a sociological survey of Almaty residents.

The fieldwork was conducted from 18 February to 11 March 2026, with a sample of 1,000 respondents; the sample is representative of the city’s adult population (aged 18 and above) by gender, age, and district of residence and covers all eight administrative districts of the city. The statistical margin of error does not exceed ±3.
1 percentage points at a 95% confidence level; the margin of error is higher for subsamples such as individual districts and age groups.

The profile consists of four sub-indices measuring different dimensions of awareness: affective (emotional perception of the threat), cognitive (knowledge and awareness), conative (attitudes and willingness to act), active — actual practices.

The methodology follows the approaches set out in the Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (OECD / Joint Research Centre of the European Commission; Nardo et al., 2005). The Index measures the social perception of risk and does not replace environmental monitoring data.

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: Key Findings The overall Index score and profile stand at 41.2 out of 100, corresponding to the category “low level, predominantly passive attitude”. The profile shows a consistent decline in engagement as the progression

moves from emotions to action: high concern (70.4) does not translate into knowledge (37.6), willingness to act (40.2), or actual practices (16.8). The gap between concern and action is 53.5 points, making it the defining feature of the current situation.
Key observations: 1. 81% of respondents consider the state of air quality dangerous to
health, up from 74%, while 63% report a high level of concern about the
issue. 2. Despite the availability of air quality monitoring tools, awareness of
them remains limited. Only 20% of respondents know where they can
check air quality, while 62% have not heard of any relevant platforms. At the
same time, official air quality data are used by only around 5% of
respondents. 3. Support for different measures declines substantially as the personal
costs associated with them increase. Systemic measures whose
implementation falls primarily on the government, or the energy sector
receive relatively high levels of support: development of public
transport – 54%, conversion of CHP plants to gas – 52%, and restrictions
on older vehicles – 51%. By contrast, measures involving additional costs or
restrictions for residents themselves receive noticeably less support, for
example, 28% of respondents support paid entry to the city center for all

vehicles. 4. The most pronounced gap is observed between concern about the problem and practical action. Only 12% of residents regularly check air quality data, almost half of respondents (46%) have taken no environmental action over the past year, and 17% use no measures to protect themselves from polluted air.

Existing practices are more strongly oriented towards adaptation to current conditions, while participation in collective initiatives, civic oversight, and support for environmental projects occurs substantially less often than respondents’ stated willingness to engage in such activities. 5.
Awareness, risk perception, and behavioral patterns vary considerably across population groups, which may limit the effectiveness of uniform communication approaches.

The chain “concern → knowledge → action” manifests differently across groups: younger respondents demonstrate higher levels of awareness but lower engagement in practical action, while older respondents are more likely to express concern but less likely to use available information sources. The most balanced indicators are

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: observed among respondents aged 25–34. The gap in knowledge of information channels between groups with different levels of education is nearly eightfold (7%
versus 56%). Having children is also associated with a higher perception of the threat posed by air pollution, regardless of respondents’ other characteristics (51% versus 42%).

Conclusion The study identifies a persistent pattern: a high level of concern about air pollution coexists with limited awareness of available information sources and a comparatively low level of practical engagement.

The findings provide a clearer understanding of residents’ attitudes towards air pollution and may serve as an additional source of evidence for the development of communication and environmental initiatives.

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: Section 2. Air Quality Awareness Index: Overall Picture 2.1. How the Index is structured The Air Quality Awareness Index aggregates four dimensions of residents’ attitudes towards air pollution, arranged in a logical sequence: affective (emotional perception of the threat) → cognitive (knowledge and awareness) → conative (attitudes and willingness to act) → active (actual practices).
Each dimension is assessed on a scale from 0 to 100, while the overall Index is

calculated as the average of the four sub-indices (see Section 8 for methodology). The overall Index score is interpreted according to the following scale: 0–25 — extremely low level, 26–50 — low level, predominantly passive attitude, 51–75 — pronounced concern with limited activity, 76–100 — high level of awareness and active behavior.

How to interpret Index scores The Index measures public awareness and attitudes, not actual air quality. Higher score indicates stronger recognition of the problem, more comprehensive knowledge, or more active behavior.
This leads to a general interpretation rule applied throughout the sections below: for each indicator, a higher score is assigned to the response reflecting a higher level of awareness.
For the assessment of air quality in the respondent’s area of residence (indicator A1), this means that a negative assessment receives a higher score than a positive one.

A resident who assesses air quality as poor recognizes the existence of the problem; an assessment of “good” where actual pollution levels exceed regulatory standards indicates that the problem has not been recognized. The second interpretation rule concerns the overall score.
The Index is calculated as the simple average of the four sub-indices, meaning that the same overall score may reflect very different combinations of dimensions.

A score of 41 may result either from uniformly moderate values across all four sub-indices or, as in the present case, from a high affective dimension combined with an extremely low active dimension. The structure of the profile therefore carries more substantive meaning than the overall score alone. For this reason, Section 2.
2 examines the sub-indices separately, while Sections 3–6 analyze each dimension individually.

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: 2.2. Overall Index Score The overall Air Quality Awareness Index score for Almaty is 41.2 out of 100. This corresponds to the category “low level, predominantly passive attitude.”

The city is positioned near the upper boundary of this range but does not reach the “pronounced concern with limited activity” category (51–75). Fuller picture is provided by the four sub-indices shown below.
Sub-index Score Interpretation category Affective – emotional perception of the 70,3 threat
medium/high Cognitive — knowledge and awareness 37,6 low Conative — attitudes and willingness to
40,2 low act Active — actual practices Overall Awareness Index

16,8 extremely low 41,2 low The profile shows a broadly declining pattern along the chain “threat perception → knowledge → willingness → action.” The following changes are observed at each transition between dimensions: ● from emotional perception of the threat (affect) to knowledge and awareness (cognition): a decline of 32.7 points.

Emotional recognition of the problem is not supported by sufficient knowledge, most concerned residents do not know where to check air quality: 62% do not know where to access such information (Section 4),
while 56% are unaware of any initiatives currently being implemented (Section 4).

● from knowledge and awareness (cognition) to willingness to act (conation): an increase of 2.6 points. Existing knowledge is translated into stated attitudes and intentions; attitudes are therefore not the main bottleneck in the profile.

● from willingness to act to actual action: a decline of 23.4 points, from 40.2 to 16.8. Stated willingness does not translate into actual practices: 46.4% took no environmental action over the past year, while 16.8% use no

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: measures to protect themselves from polluted air (Section 6). The gap between the affective and active dimensions is 53.5 points, which is the defining characteristic of the
current profile. In other words, the high level of concern about air pollution (70.3) is not accompanied by a comparable level of practical action among residents (16.8).

2.3. Interpretation of the Profile The structure of the profile supports three main conclusions, which are examined in greater detail in the following sections. First, the lack of awareness is driven not by a lack of interest in the issue, but by a shortage of practical information.

The affective dimension is the only component within the medium-to-high range: most residents perceive air pollution as a serious threat to health (81.1% consider it dangerous or very dangerous), while 57.2% of respondents considering relocation cite air quality as the main reason for this decision.

The problem is therefore already perceived as significant and potentially dangerous. At the same time, a high level of concern is not always accompanied by sufficient knowledge of the causes of pollution, available data sources, and possible ways to respond (Section 8).
Second, the main constraints are concentrated in the cognitive and active dimensions. The low cognitive sub-index score is largely driven by limited awareness of how to check air

quality (indicator B1 — 29.1) and of existing initiatives (B3 — 29.9). Knowledge of pollution sources is more developed (B2 — 53.8), although the findings indicate certain distortions in how these sources are perceived (Section 4). The low active sub-index score (16.

8) reflects the infrequent practice of regularly checking air quality data (D1 – 14.4), limited use of protective measures (D2 – 23.7), and low engagement in environmental action (D3 – 12.2). Third, a high level of concern coexists with limited knowledge and practical action. The gap between the affective and active dimensions is 53.

5 points: the affective sub-index reaches 70.3, while the active sub-index stands at only 16.8. This indicates a substantial gap between perceptions of the air pollution problem and the actual level of engagement in actions aimed at addressing it.
Where access to clear and relevant information sources is limited, perceptions of the problem may be shaped to a greater extent by personal experience and informal communication channels.
2.4. Trends: Comparison with the 2024–2025 Surveys The current survey is the first in which the Air Quality Awareness Index has been calculated. However, changes in
public perceptions can be assessed using comparable individual

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: Taken together, the indicators show differing trends across the components. Cognitive indicators are improving gradually, albeit from a very low base: knowledge of air quality monitoring channels has doubled over two years but still reaches only one fifth of the population.

Affective indicators have stabilized at a high level, while behavioral indicators show no comparable improvement. The gap between awareness and action should therefore be regarded as not yet narrowing, and its magnitude may

serve as a target indicator for assessing the effectiveness of the city’s information and environmental policies. Sections 3–6 examine each of the four dimensions in sequence, covering the sub-index score, the distribution of responses across the respective indicators, and differences between socio-demographic and territorial groups.
Section 7 brings these differences together into group profiles.

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: Section 3. Affective Dimension: Emotional Perception of the Problem
3.1. Sub-index score and indicator structure Affective sub-index measures population’s emotional response to air pollution: assessment of air quality in
the area of residence, a degree of personal concern, and perception of health risks.
Indicator A1 A2 A3 Sub-index Description Score Assessment of air quality in the area of 62,1 residence
Degree of personal concern about the issue 69,0 Assessment of the health risks posed by 80,0 air pollution
70,3 The score of 70.3 is the highest among the four sub-indices and the only one falling within the medium-to-high range. Clear gradient is observed within the sub-index: perception of health risks

(A3) produces the highest score, while assessment of air quality in one’s own area (A1) is more moderate. Residents perceive the overall threat as more severe than the situation in their immediate surroundings.

3.2. Assessment of air quality (indicator A1) According to the current survey, 30.6% of respondents rate air quality in their area of residence as “poor” and 18.8% as “very poor.” Overall, 49.4% provide a negative assessment. Neutral
assessment (“satisfactory”) is given by 31.8%, while 17.9% provide a positive assessment (“good” — 15.5%, “very good” — 2.4%).

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: Share of negative assessments increased from 42% in 2024 to 50% in 2025 and has stabilized at approximately this level in the current wave.

This increase may reflect not so much an actual deterioration in air quality as growing awareness: as residents become better informed about the issue (Section 4), they may begin to assess familiar conditions more critically. Marked differences are observed across districts. Negative assessments dominate (≥50%) in the Almaly

(64.6%), Zhetysu (54.2%), Auezov (52.9%), and Bostandyk (50.0%) districts. The most favorable perceptions are found in Nauryzbay District, where 65.7% rate air quality as satisfactory or better, while the share giving the most negative assessment, “very poor,” is the lowest at 8.8%.
The highest proportion of extremely negative assessments is recorded in Zhetysu District, where 31.3% describe air quality as “very poor,” approximately twice the citywide level.
3.3. Personal concern (indicator A2) Air pollution concerns 31.3% of residents “very strongly” and 32.2% “strongly,” bringing the combined level of pronounced concern to 63.5%.
Neutral position is reported by 22.6%, while 13.3% are little or not at all concerned.

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: The overall level of pronounced concern remains unchanged from the summer 2025 wave (63%), indicating that the affective background has stabilized at a high level following the increase observed between the 2024 and 2025 waves. The age pattern of concern is non-linear.

The highest levels of “very strong” concern are recorded among economically active middle-age groups: 39.1% among those aged 35–44 and 35.5% among those aged 25–34. The lowest level is among respondents aged 18–24 (15.1%), more than twice as low as among middle-aged respondents. The 65+ group is also below the overall average (23.9%).

Thus, the issue is felt most acutely by the working-age population, which also experiences the greatest symptom burden (Section 6). Differences are also observed across Almaty districts. Residents of Bostandyk and Zhetysu districts report the highest levels of concern: 43.4% and 33.7%, respectively, selected “very strongly concerned”.

By contrast, only 28.4% of residents in Nauryzbay District and 26.3% in Turksib District reported the same level of concern. Strong concern increases with education level: among residents with secondary education or below, 27.4% report strong concern; among those with higher education, the figure is 34.
1%; and among holders of academic degrees, it reaches 44.4%, the highest level.
Having children also substantially increases concern: among parents of
children under 18, 41.3% are “very strongly” concerned about air
pollution, compared with only 24.8% among respondents without
children. A consistent pattern is observed across the different
socio-demographic dimensions: concern increases with income,
education, and having children. In other words, the more resources an
individual has, the more seriously they tend to perceive the problem. This has
two implications that become apparent in later sections. On the one
hand, better-resourced groups are more active than others in protecting
themselves from pollution (Section 6). On the other hand, they are also more

likely to consider moving away (Section 3.5). Comparison of the territorial patterns for A1 and A2 reveals a geographical mismatch: the district with the highest concern, Bostandyk, is not among those with the worst perceived air quality, whereas Turksib and Nauryzbay, despite substantial actual exposure associated with private housing and industrial zones, display the lowest levels of concern.

The affective response is therefore shaped not only by actual pollution levels but also by the socio-economic characteristics of district residents. More affluent districts tend to express greater concern even where environmental conditions are comparable or better, while districts

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: facing objectively higher exposure report lower levels of concern.

3.4. Perception of health risks (indicator A3) Risk perception is the highest-scoring component of the affective dimension. Air pollution is considered “very dangerous” to health by 45.6% of residents and “rather dangerous” by another 35.5%, (total 81.1%), a further 11.5% give an intermediate assessment, describing pollution as “dangerous in some respects but not

in others,” while 6.4% do not perceive a significant threat (“rather not dangerous” — 4.8%, “not dangerous at all” — 1.6%). Compared with the 2025 wave, the combined share rating air pollution as “dangerous/very dangerous” increased from 74% to 81.1%. This is the only affective indicator that continues to rise while the others have stabilized.

Risk perception also differs across social groups. ● Having children increases perceived risk: among parents of minors, 51.1% consider air pollution “very dangerous,” compared with 41.8% among respondents without children. ● By age, the highest shares of “very dangerous” assessments are

found among respondents aged 35–44 (51.1%) and 55–64 (50.8%), while the lowest are among those aged 18–24 (36.3%) and 65+ (35.1%). The parental perspective therefore strengthens risk perception beyond age differences and may provide one of the most universal frames for public communication.
3.5. Behavioral consequences of emotional perception: migration intentions
Within the structure of the report, extreme manifestation of the affective migration intentions are treated as an dimension: intention to leave the city

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: represents the strongest form of response to a perceived threat and, unlike indicators of the active dimension, does not require everyday behavioral practices. One in four residents is seriously considering leaving Almaty: 21.0% think about relocation frequently and discuss it with their family, 2.8% have a firm decision and 2.1% are in the

process of moving. Combined, these groups account for 25.9% of respondents. A further 32.4% have considered moving but have no specific plans, while only 41.3% have never considered leaving. The indicator has risen relative to previous waves, but the increase occurred between the 2024 and 2025 waves: 17% in 2024, 25% in 2025 and 25.

9% in the current wave. Air pollution is the most frequently cited reason for potential relocation: 57.2% of those considering moving name it as the main reason, far ahead of low income and limited career prospects (22.8%) and the desire to provide a better future for their children (20.6%).

At the same time, these intentions are largely reversible: among potential migrants, 50.1% would abandon plans to relocate if air quality improved significantly, whereas for 48.0% such an improvement would not be decisive. As for preferred destinations, countries outside the near region account for the largest share (26.

7%), followed by other cities in Kazakhstan (24.2%). Among respondents not concerned at all about air pollution, 61.7% have never considered leaving Almaty, while only 16.7% seriously consider relocation: 11.7% think about it and 5.0% have a firm decision or are in the process of moving, among those strongly concerned, 39.0% seriously consider relocation: 31.6% think about it frequently, 4.

2% have firm decision, and 3.2% are in the process of moving. The relationship between the share of potential migrants and the level of concern provides direct quantitative evidence of the link between the affective dimension and migration intentions. Socio-demographic differentiation:

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: ● Education. The higher the level of education, the more frequently respondents consider relocation: among holders of master’s or academic degrees, 40.7% either frequently consider leaving, have already decided to leave, or are preparing to relocate. This is twice the share among respondents with secondary education (20.2%). ● Age.

Relocation is considered most frequently by respondents aged 25–34 — 40.2% (based on the share of the three responses indicating intention to leave), the lowest share is recorded among respondents aged 65+ (10.4%).
● Children. Among parents with one or two children, 28–30% consider
relocation, compared with 23% among respondents without children.

Seasonal migration is widespread among those who are generally open to leaving, including 54.5% would like to leave the city during the winter if they had the opportunity, and 15.0% already do so every year, this amounts to 69.5%, while for 30.5% this is not typical.
The highest share of residents who either wish to leave the city for the winter or already do so every year is found among those most concerned about air pollution: 19.0% and 61.9%,
respectively. The highest share of residents who neither leave nor plan to leave for the winter, 60.9%, is recorded among those who are not concerned at all about air pollution in Almaty.

3.6. Conclusions on the affective dimension The affective sub-index (70.3) is the only component of the Index within the medium-to-high range and is what keeps the overall score near the upper boundary of the “low” category. The affective background has stabilized: following the increase between the 2024 and 2025 waves,

the shares of negative assessments and pronounced concern have remained unchanged, while only the perception of health risks continues to rise (74% → 81.1%). Concern is concentrated among working-age middle-aged groups and is further strengthened by parenthood.

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: Migration intentions are directly linked to affect and are largely reversible: more than half of potential migrants would remain in the city if air quality improved, making air quality not only an environmental factor but also a demographic factor in the city’s long-term sustainability.

The affective dimension is the highest-scoring component of the profile. Section 4 examines the second link in the chain: the extent to which strong threat perception is accompanied by knowledge of the causes of pollution, ways to check air quality, and initiatives currently being implemented.

blocks: Section 4. Cognitive Dimension: Knowledge and Awareness 4.1. Sub-index score and indicator structure
The cognitive sub-index measures public awareness: knowledge of where and how to check air quality,
perceptions of the main sources of pollution, and awareness of initiatives currently being implemented.
Indicator B1 B2 B3 Sub-index Description Score Knowledge of where and how to 29,1 check air quality
Perceptions of the main sources 53,8 of pollution Knowledge of specific initiatives 29,9 to improve air quality

37,6 The cognitive sub-index is separated from the affective sub-index by the largest gap in the profile — 32.7 points. The internal structure of this dimension is uneven: relatively well-developed perceptions of pollution sources coexist with limited

knowledge of monitoring tools and existing initiatives. Residents have a general understanding of causes of the problem but have limited access to data on its current state and to information about measures being implemented.
4.2. Knowledge of air quality monitoring channels (indicator B1)

20.4% of respondents confidently know where to check air quality, 17.4% have heard something about available sources but are unsure and 62.2% do not know. Awareness has steadily improved: the share who know where to check air quality rose from 10% in 2024 to 20.4%, while the uninformed share fell from 74% to 62.2%. Nevertheless, the

baseline remains low: four out of five residents still do not have confident access to air quality data, even though monitoring tools, including public maps, mobile applications, and AAI’s independent sensor network, have become substantially more accessible over the same period.
In other words, the problem is not the absence of tools, but the fact that people are unaware of them.

chunks.title: Public perceptions of air quality in Almaty: third annual study (reviewed by PwC)
blocks: The trend across survey waves represents the most consistent positive development observed in the study:
