chunks.title: Study of Public Attitudes Toward the Introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZ) in Almaty
blocks: The Almaty Air Initiative Foundation conducted a sociological study to determine whether Almaty residents perceive transport as a source of air pollution and the idea of introducing Low Emission Zones (LEZ).
The results show that a majority of residents support the idea (51%), but support is uneven and depends on mode of transport, income, gender, and district of residence.

Methodology The study was conducted using an online survey. A total of 500 Almaty residents aged 18 and above participated, selected with consideration for gender and key transport groups: pedestrians and public transport users (200 people), car owners (200 people), taxi drivers (100 people). The questionnaire included both closed-ended questions,
allowing for quantitative assessment of awareness and attitudes toward LEZ, and open-ended questions, capturing personal comments.
The analysis was carried out taking into account respondents’ socio-demographic characteristics, including age, income, marital status, presence of children, loans, and district of residence.
How concerned are Almaty residents about air quality? 88% of respondents stated that they are concerned about air quality in Almaty.
Concern is particularly high among: • women (88%), • families with children (90%). Among women, having children significantly increases concern:

90% of mothers are concerned, compared to 79% of women without children. Among men, the difference is almost negligible: 88% of fathers and 87% of men without children equally consider air quality a problem.

chunks.title: Study of Public Attitudes Toward the Introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZ) in Almaty
blocks: • By district: Medeu District — 92%, Auezov and Turksib Districts — 90% each.
Concern about air quality is an universal issue. Even among those who are skeptical about LEZ, the majority (88%) are still concerned about air pollution.
Transport as a main source of pollution Nearly half of respondents (around 50%) consider transport to be the main source of air pollution:
1% identify passenger cars as the main culprit, 9% point to freight transport.

Breakdown by mode of mobility reveals notable differences in perception. Among respondents who mostly walk or use bicycles, scooters, or mopeds, nearly half (45.5%) consider passenger cars the main source of pollution, and another 9% highlight freight transport.
Among public transport users, nearly half (47%) also consider cars the main source of pollution, about 5% mention trucks, and around 23% point to industrial enterprises and thermal power plants.

Among car owners, however, only 34% acknowledge the contribution of passenger cars to air pollution, and another 13% blame trucks. Most shift responsibility to thermal power plants and industrial facilities (21%), construction (19%), which indicates an underestimation of the impact of personal vehicles on urban air pollution.
The issue of older cars (over 15 years old, manufactured before 2010) has become a key dividing line in society.

chunks.title: Study of Public Attitudes Toward the Introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZ) in Almaty
blocks: • Among owners of older cars 21% agree that their vehicles pollute, while an overwhelming majority (66%) disagree.
Among owners of newer cars, the situation is reversed: nearly 59% acknowledge that older vehicles significantly pollute urban air.
This suggests that owners of older cars are less likely to recognize their contribution to air pollution.

Similar pattern was observed in the private housing sector: homeowners tend not to recognize that their stoves and fuel significantly contribute to air pollution. In respondents’ answers, other sources ranked higher in importance, while coal burning in private homes was only fourth among pollution sources.
It is also notable that when choosing a car, environmental factors are hardly considered: price, convenience, and time remain the top priorities, rather than environmental impact.
Some respondents (24%) point to other major sources of pollution: thermal power plants, construction, industrial emissions, etc.

Overall conclusion: nearly every second pedestrian or public transport user directly blames cars, while car owners are far more likely to shift responsibility to external factors. A clear trend emerges: the more a person depends on a private car, the less willing they are to recognize it as the main source of pollution.

Old cars and LEZ: conflict of interests On average, 51% of respondents are willing to support the introduction of LEZ. There are relatively few outright opponents (18%), but they are concentrated within specific groups.

chunks.title: Study of Public Attitudes Toward the Introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZ) in Almaty
blocks: LEZ supporters: • Owners of newer cars (no older than 10 years) are the most pro-LEZ group (65% support).

• People with higher incomes primarily associate LEZ with expected health benefits: cleaner air, fewer illnesses, and a safer environment for families. This group shows a high level of support (61%), whereas among middle- and lower-income groups, support is only around half (48% and 50%, respectively).

• Respondents aged 56+ also demonstrate strong support — around 60%. For this group, environmental and health impacts are particularly important, with mentions of asthma, allergies, and lack of oxygen.
• Taxi drivers are mostly in favor of LEZ — 59% respondents supported the initiative.
• Pedestrians, public transport users, and taxi users as a group show 52% support.

• Women are more likely to support LEZ (51% pro and only 13% cons). Their main motivation is the health of their families and children. Men show a similar level of support (51%), but are more skeptical: share of opponents among them is almost twice as high (21% opposed).
At the same time, men with families demonstrate higher support (52%), highlighting the importance of concern for loved ones.
• Residents living in central and southern districts (Almaly, Bostandyk), where traffic load is higher, are also more supportive.

chunks.title: Study of Public Attitudes Toward the Introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZ) in Almaty
blocks: The main arguments are health, clean air, and desire to remove old, “smoking” vehicles. Most of them perceive LEZ as an investment in the future and are willing to accept gradual implementation, understanding that the effects will not be immediate.
There are also “passive supporters” — those not directly affected by the measure and who do not oppose it.
Opponents and skeptics: • Among private car owners, support for LEZ is below average: 44% pros and 27% cons.
• Owners of older cars are the most critical group: only 26% support LEZ, while 39% oppose it.
Key arguments of owners of old cars against the LEZ are primarily related to the sense of unfairness (66%) and concerns about additional costs (35%).
Nearly half of respondents (45%) explicitly state that LEZ implementation should be accompanied by: development of public transport, programs for replacing old vehicles.

There are also doubts that removing some vehicles will significantly improve air quality: some respondents point to the combined impact of other sources (thermal power plants, construction, industrial emissions).

In most groups, supporters of LEZ outnumber opponents. However, owners of older vehicles form the core of resistance: for them, this is not an environmental measure, but a threat to their budget and way of life.

chunks.title: Study of Public Attitudes Toward the Introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZ) in Almaty
blocks: Open-ended responses LEZ supporters: “That’s very good: we’ll breathe clean air, children will get sick less.”
“Environmental conditions will improve, and there will be fewer health problems in winter when coal-fired plants operate.”

“If low emission zones are introduced in Almaty, it will positively affect my family’s health: breathing will become easier, especially for people with allergies and children. Noise and dust from transport will also decrease, and the city will become more comfortable for walking.”
“In our family, everyone has allergies — rhinitis, hives. Noise and constant traffic make life uncomfortable. If there are fewer cars, it will be easier to breathe and health will improve.”
“There will be fewer cars and traffic jams, therefore air will be cleaner.”
“My and my relatives’ well-being would improve, and traffic congestion would decrease.”
“It may become harder to get around, as public transport will be crowded, but we will tolerate it. Just start doing something. We can’t wait any longer.”
LEZ opponents: “Why should I pay to move around my own city if my car complies with inspection standards?”

chunks.title: Study of Public Attitudes Toward the Introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZ) in Almaty
blocks: “It will hit our budget.” “I’ll have to replace my car, but we can’t afford it yet.”
“I will protest.” “It won’t change anything — everything will still be stolen.”
“Until urban development and corruption issues are resolved, I am opposed to it.”
“It will become inconvenient to move around the city. Create a program to exchange old cars for new ones with co-financing, zero interest, and 20-year installments.”
“I will lose my client base, and the cost of my services will increase.”

Expectations from LEZ Nearly half of respondents associate LEZ with an improvement in quality of life: 47% expect that it will lead to cleaner air in Almaty. Perceived benefits include reduced traffic load, fleet renewal, incentives to switch to public transport.

The study confirms that the introduction of LEZ in Almaty can rely on public support. Residents are generally ready to support LEZ if they see real improvements — cleaner air and better quality of life.

However, some respondents expressed concerns: they were worried about maintaining the family budget, their usual mobility, and possible corruption risks. Another key success factor is integrating LEZ into a comprehensive approach, addressing transport, infrastructure, and industrial emissions simultaneously.

chunks.title: Study of Public Attitudes Toward the Introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZ) in Almaty
blocks: What residents expect first: • Development of public transport and alternative mobility – buses, metro, cycling infrastructure.
• Vehicle scrappage and exchange programs with compensation and benefits. Quote: “If the government helps people get rid of old cars and buy newer or new ones, then this would work for us.”
• Fair rules that apply to everyone. • Open and clear communication from the authorities.
Conclusion Support for low emission zones in Almaty largely depends on how the measures are implemented and perceived by residents.

The study shows that most residents are concerned about air quality, and nearly half associate LEZ with hope for cleaner air. Supporters include owners of relatively new cars, taxi drivers, pedestrians, taxi users, public transport users, women, and families with children.

Among owners of older vehicles, skepticism remains higher. However, it is crucial to show this group that LEZ is not just a restriction, but an opportunity to make Almaty a modern city where clean air becomes the norm and a right for everyone.

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: On December 30, 2025, Almaty adopted the Atmospheric Air Protection Rules, which provide for further restrictions on motor vehicles. In response, the Almaty Air Initiative is conducting a study to assess the impact of the city’s vehicle fleet structure on air quality.
Motor vehicles are a key source of air pollution in Almaty, particularly in terms of nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate matter.

In response to this challenge, the city is considering system-wide measures to reduce vehicle emissions, including the introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZs), primarily targeting vehicles in emission classes 0-4 – the segment of the vehicle fleet with the highest pollutant emissions.

This study assesses the contribution of motor vehicles to air pollution in Almaty, focusing on fine particles (PM2.5) and nitrogen oxides. The paper analyzes the structure of the city’s vehicle fleet, the actual distribution of traffic flows, and how vehicles of different emission classes contribute to air pollution.

The study also models the potential impact of introducing low-emission zones. The objective of the study is to estimate the potential environmental impact of restrictions on the city’s most polluting vehicles.

Nitrogen Dioxide Pollution Motor traffic remains a key source of air pollution in Almaty. More than 600,000 vehicles operate in the city daily, making transport the primary contributor to nitrogen dioxide (NO2) emissions.
According to a 2024 study by the Almaty Air Initiative, average annual NO2 concentrations in the city exceed WHO (World Health Organization) recommendations:

• by a factor of 6.1 in 2023 • by a factor of 5.9 in 2024 These levels of exposure document adverse health effects. According to the WHO, long-term exposure to elevated NO2 concentration causes decreased lung function, exacerbates asthma, and increases the incidence of hospitalizations related to respiratory diseases.

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: Traffic-Related Air Pollution (TRAP) and Its Impact on Health

Air quality near roads differs significantly from background levels. This is why scientific literature uses a separate term for traffic-related air pollution: TRAP (Traffic-related air pollution). TRAP is a mixture of gases and particles formed directly in road corridors: nitrogen dioxide (NO2), PM2.

5, PM10, soot, volatile organic compounds, and other toxic components. Pollution is generated not only by engine operation but also by tire wear, brake wear, and road surface abrasions. A significant portion of the emissions are concentrated at breathing height, which increases their harmful effects.
International studies show a consistent link between TRAP, particularly high NO2 concentrations and proximity to roads, and:
• increased risk of developing asthma in adults and children
• increased risk of cardiovascular disease • increased overall mortality
• increased risk of lung cancer According to WHO estimates, approximately 16% of childhood asthma cases in cities are directly related to exposure to NO2 – a major transport pollutant.

Residents of areas near heavy traffic are at greatest risk. Living within 100-500 meters of busy roads carries an increased risk of childhood asthma, pregnancy complications, and long-term cognitive effects associated with chronic exposure to NO2 and PM2.5.

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: A particular feature of traffic pollution is its increased impact on road users. A study of fine particle concentrations on roads found that drivers and passengers stuck in traffic with the open windows breathe air seven times more polluted than pedestrians standing at intersections.
Furthermore, air pollution inside a car stuck in traffic is 40% higher than under free-flowing traffic conditions.

The scale of the impact of transport pollution is often underestimated. In several countries, including Australia, mortality associated with vehicle emissions significantly exceeds the number of fatalities in road accidents. Globally, transport emissions are associated with approximately 246,000 premature deaths annually.

Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Over the past year, Almaty has become one of the fastest-growing cities in the region in terms of vehicle ownership. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Kazakhstan, as of September 2025, 797,000 vehicles were registered in the city, which is almost 150,000 more than the year before (647,000).

Of these, 714,000 were passenger cars. The number of electric vehicles is also growing rapidly: their number has almost doubled in one year, from 6,410 to 12,401. However, their share of the city’s vehicle fleet remains small, at around 2%. Hybrids* account for 4% of the vehicle fleet.
*Hybrids are cars with multiple fuel types: gasoline, gas and electricity.
Vehicle’s Age is a Key Factor in Air Quality The structure of the city’s registered vehicle fleet reveals a serious problem:
• 25% of cars are between 10 and 20 years old • 30% are over 20 years old

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: In the Almaty region, the situation is even worse: 57% of cars are over 20 years old.
Age is an indirect indicator of the environmental class of a vehicle – the older the car, the lower its environmental class, and the more emissions it produces.

What’s Really Happening on the Roads? To get a realistic picture of traffic, analysts from Almaty Air Initiative and Sergek Group studied traffic flows for a year – from August 1, 2024, to August 1, 2025. A total of 1.8 million unique vehicles were analyzed.
Structure by type of vehicle • 90% – passenger cars • 8% – trucks
• 2% – buses Age structure by vehicle flow • 33% – manufactured in 2021 or newer
In fact, every third car on the city streets (33%) is older than 15 years (made before 2010).
Low Emission Zone (LEZ) Pilot Analysis Results To assess the potential impact of the Low Emission Zone, a block of the following streets was studied: Kabanbay Batyr – Dostyk – Abay – Zheltoksan.

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: Period: October 1–29, 2025. On average, approximately 82,000 unique vehicles pass through the zone daily.
Structure by type of vehicle: • 95% – passenger cars • 4% – trucks
• <1% – buses Age structure: • 63% – under 10 years old. • 37% – eco-class 0-4.
Thus, cars of eco-class 5 accounts for 63% of the total mileage in the block, while vehicles in eco-classes 0-4 make up only 37%:
To assess the contribution of various vehicle fleet segments to air pollution, vehicle emissions within the studied area were calculated by vehicle type and emission class.
The calculations were performed using emission factors from the COPERT methodology, widely used in European and international vehicle emission inventories, together with total vehicle mileage data.
Although vehicles in emission classes 0-4 account for only 37% of the total mileage, they account for 79% of NOx emissions and 78% of PM emissions from vehicles within the studied area.
This confirms the general pattern established by international agencies: older and technically obsolete engines emit significantly more NOx and fine particles per kilometer traveled.

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: When considering the contribution by transport type, with a share of 3% of the total mileage, trucks account for 32% of NOx emissions and 64% of PM, highlighting their disproportionately high contribution to vehicle pollution.

Hypothetical Scenario for Vehicle Fleet Modernization Modeling has shown that if all vehicles in emission classes 0–4 were upgraded to Euro-5, while maintaining the current mileage within the pilot zone, a significant reduction in transport emissions would be achieved:
• a 67% reduction in NOx emissions • a 62% reduction in PM emissions

Taking a more targeted approach, even modernization of trucks only yields a significant impact due to their high disproportionate pollutant contribution. With a relatively small share of miles traveled, emission reductions can go up to 15% of NOx emissions and 50% of PM emissions.
However, the greatest potential for reducing vehicle pollution lies not so much in fleet renewal as in the transition to eco-friendly public transport.

In addition to modernizing trucks, a complete transition of passengers from private cars to electric-powered public transport simultaneously reduces both the total number of kilometers traveled and pollution, achieving an 83% reduction in NOx emissions and an 86% reduction in PM emissions.
The assessment reflects the total emissions of vehicles within the studied area and illustrates the potential impact of upgrading the most polluting segment of the vehicle fleet.
Why is This Important? • Air pollution from transport is one of the main reasons for elevated NO2 levels in Almaty.

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: • According to the WHO, NO2 and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) are associated with an increase in asthma in children, worsening of cardiovascular diseases and an increased risk of overall mortality.

International experience shows that vehicle fleet renewal and the introduction of Low Emission Zones (LEZs) are effective tools for reducing transport pollution. Such measures have been implemented in London, Paris, Berlin, Madrid, and more than 300 cities in Europe and Asia.
A case in point is Bradford (UK), where the LEZ was used as a tool for accelerated transport modernization. Between 2022 and 2024:
• 87% of taxis switched to stricter environmental standards,
• 370 city buses were modernized, • 33 electric buses were purchased.

This case demonstrates that the LEZ can function not as a prohibitive measure, but as an economic and regulatory incentive, accelerating fleet renewal and the development of environmentally friendly public transport without major social disruption.

The most sustainable long-term effect is achieved by reducing the use of private cars and developing high-quality, environmentally friendly public transport. The transition from private to public transport simultaneously reduces emissions, road congestion, and the impact of transport-related air pollution (TRAP) on the population.
In a highly motorized context, fleet renewal and the introduction of LEZs are essential transitional measures that can achieve short-term reductions in harmful impacts.

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: The results of the study reveal a critical imbalance: the bulk of toxic air pollution in Almaty is generated not by the overall flow of vehicles, but by a specific segment of the fleet.

Vehicles in emission classes 0–4, while accounting for only 39% of the total mileage, are responsible for 79% of nitrogen oxide emissions, creating a “traffic trap” (TRAP), where city residents are exposed to NO2 and PM2.5 concentrations that are several times above WHO recommendations.

Modeling shows that targeted interventions on this segment of the vehicle fleet — through modernization, replacement, or operating restrictions — can reduce overall vehicle emissions in the city by up to half. Reducing NO2 and PM2.
5 emissions is directly linked to reduced public health risks, particularly for respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.

This very effect was observed in the aforementioned Bradford (UK) example: just one year after the launch of the Low Emission Zone (LEZ), resulting in 700 fewer doctor visits per month: 600 for respiratory diseases and 134 for cardiovascular diseases.
This experience confirms that low emission zones can deliver rapid and measurable health benefits, not just reduced emissions.

Therefore, low-emission zones are an effective tool for comprehensively addressing transport pollution: firstly, they reduce concentrations of toxic gases and fine particles by restricting the most polluting transport; secondly, they stimulate fleet renewal, accelerating the transition to electric vehicles and low-emission transport without direct bans; and thirdly, they provide a measurable effect on public health.

Conclusion The study shows that the decisive factor in air pollution in Almaty is not the total number of vehicles, but the quality of the vehicle fleet. Approximately 49% of vehicles belonging to older emission classes contribute disproportionately to nitrogen oxide (NOx) and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) emissions.

chunks.title: Not the Quantity, but the Quality: How the Structure of Almaty’s Vehicle Fleet Affects Air Quality
blocks: In the long term, achieving safe air quality is impossible without developing high-quality public transportation and reducing the city’s reliance on private cars. However, given the high level of motorization, transitional measures are needed to reduce the impact of the most polluting segment of the vehicle fleet.

Such measures may include low-emission zones (LEZs) and other tools aimed at upgrading, replacing, or restricting the use of vehicles with low emission ratings. A targeted approach to this segment allows for rapid and significant reductions in the impact of transport pollution without applying blanket restrictions to the entire vehicle population.

Scenario analysis shows that the gradual replacement or decommissioning of the most polluting vehicles could reduce NOx and PM2.5 emissions by more than 60%. Therefore, regulation focused on the environmental performance of transport is a justified and effective step in bringing air quality in Almaty to levels safe for public health.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: PM2.5 Monitoring Results: Key Figures 2025 was another challenging year for Almaty residents in terms of air quality. We recorded a 30% increase in pollutant concentrations compared with the previous year.

The main sources of air pollution in Almaty have not changed significantly in recent years. Much of the year-to-year variation can be explained by weather conditions. In 2024, a windier winter and a rainy summer acted as a natural filter, bringing the annual average PM2.5 concentration down to 24.1 µg/m³.

In 2025, precipitation was noticeably lower: a dry summer and frequent periods of calm winds during winter reduced pollutant dispersion and contributed to their accumulation. As a result, the number of polluted days increased, along with the annual average PM2.5 concentration.

Urban smog is a mixture of different pollutants. In addition to PM2.5 and PM10 particulate matter, the air contains nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), sulfur dioxide (SO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), ozone (O₃), and other substances. In this report, we focus on PM2.5 as the most harmful, representative, and readily available indicator of air pollution.
Key Indicators: • Annual average PM2.5 concentration: 31.2 µg/m³, or 6.3 times the WHO guideline.
• Worsening trend: Air pollution increased by 30% compared with 2024 (24.1 µg/m³).

• Individual health burden: The average city resident was exposed to a toxic pollution burden equivalent to smoking 518 cigarettes over the year. In Turksib District, air pollution exposure was comparable to smoking 776 cigarettes per resident.

• Shortage of clean-air days: The number of “safe” days (according to WHO guidelines) decreased by 16 compared with the previous year, from 164 days in 2024 to 148 days in 2025. This now represents only 40% of the year, compared with approximately 45% the year before.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: • The “trapping” effect: The nighttime mountain breeze does not clean the city’s air. Instead, it effectively pushes smog into lower-lying districts, where it becomes trapped due to temperature inversions.

Extremes and Contrasts: • Annual variation: Air pollution levels differed by a factor of 29 between the cleanest day (October 1) and the most polluted day (December 7). The city experiences extreme fluctuations in air quality.

• Seasonal gap: The most polluted month (December, 62.4 µg/m³) had PM2.5 concentrations 5.5 times higher than the cleanest month (May, 11.3 µg/m³). On average, PM2.5 concentrations during winter months are five times higher than during summer months.

• Geographic inequality: Turksib District (46.8 µg/m³) was 2.1 times more polluted than Bostandyk District (22.1 µg/m³). This confirms that residents of the city’s lower-lying areas face a disproportionately high pollution burden.

Air Pollution Exposure in Cigarette Equivalents To make air quality monitoring data easier to understand, we use an internationally recognized approach that converts PM2.5 concentrations into “cigarette equivalents.”
Although inhaling smog is not identical to smoking cigarettes in terms of chemical composition, it creates a comparable burden on the respiratory system, resembling continuous passive smoking.

For reference: This approach is based on estimates developed by the Berkeley Earth research group and epidemiological evidence on the health effects of PM2.5. In simplified terms, an annual average PM2.5 concentration of approximately 22 µg/m³ can be considered comparable, in terms of health risk, to smoking one cigarette per day. (Source)
Citywide estimate: In 2025, the average Almaty resident effectively “smoked” 518 cigarettes — approximately 26 packs — or nearly 1.42 cigarettes per day.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Health Risks by District: Air pollution is unevenly distributed across the city, creating different levels of long-term health risks depending on where people live:

It is important to note that, unlike active smoking, exposure to smog is continuous and involuntary. It affects the most vulnerable groups — children and the elderly — 24 hours a day, even indoors in buildings without air purification systems.

Chapter 1. Air Pollution Trends and Patterns in 2025 The annual average PM2.5 concentration in Almaty in 2025 was 31.2 µg/m³, which is 6.3 times higher than the World Health Organization (WHO) guideline of 5 µg/m³. Compared with 2024 (24.1 µg/m³), air quality deteriorated by 30%.

For reference: PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter in the air with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less. These particles are so small that they can penetrate deep into the lungs and even enter the bloodstream, making them harmful to human health. High concentrations of PM2.
5 in the air can cause respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, particularly among children, older adults, and people with chronic health conditions.
The annual pollution profile shows a strong seasonal pattern and substantial fluctuations in PM2.5 concentrations.

Winter: Characterized by extreme pollution peaks that consistently exceed Kazakhstan’s national daily average maximum permissible concentration (MPC) of 35 µg/m³. High variability and the accumulation of particulate matter near the ground create critical short-term health risks.

Spring and Summer: Pollution levels stabilize and decrease. Most readings fall within the “good” and “moderate” air quality categories, while exceedances of the MPC occur only occasionally. Nevertheless, even during favorable months, concentrations exceed the WHO daily guideline of 15 µg/m³.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Transitional Seasons: Characterized by increased variability. The alternation between clean-air days and sharp pollution spikes reflects the city’s high sensitivity to meteorological conditions and solid-fuel combustion.

Monthly Average Concentrations: 2024 vs. 2025 From January to September, Almaty operated a network of Clarity sensors installed under an Asian Development Bank program, allowing us to make a direct comparison with 2024. Comparing equivalent periods confirms the worsening air pollution trend in 2025:

Critical Increase: During the first two months of 2025, monthly average PM2.5 concentrations reached 57.5 µg/m³ in January and 61.6 µg/m³ in February, representing increases of 14% and 26%, respectively, compared with the same months in 2024.

However, March showed an improvement, with concentrations falling to 28.4 µg/m³ compared with 33.2 µg/m³ in 2024. The period from April to September traditionally remains the cleanest part of the year. Concentrations ranged from 11.3 to 15.4 µg/m³, close to the WHO daily guideline of 15 µg/m³.

Air quality follows a pronounced seasonal pattern. Even when comparing only the first nine months of the year, during which Clarity sensors had been operating for three consecutive years, 2025 showed higher pollution levels, primarily driven by winter concentrations.

Regarding the final quarter of 2025 (October–December), it is important to note that additional data sources from 170 new sensors in the Almaty Air Initiative network were included in the analysis starting in October.

The new sensors captured a sharp increase in the monthly average concentration to 36.3 µg/m³, compared with 23.1 µg/m³ in 2024. This increase was associated with the start of the heating season (October 8–10) and colder weather, which reduced pollutant dispersion.
Under these conditions, emissions accumulated in the near-surface atmospheric layer, establishing elevated background pollution levels that persisted throughout the winter.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: In November and December, concentrations reached critical levels of 54.4 µg/m³ and 62.4 µg/m³, respectively.
Number of Days Exceeding the WHO Daily Guideline In 2025, Almaty experienced a significant reduction in the number of days with safe air quality.
Over the past year, Almaty recorded 148 days (40.5% of the year) when the daily average PM2.5 concentration met the WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³ — 16 days (10%) fewer than in 2024.

During the remaining 217 days (almost 60% of the year), pollutant concentrations exceeded the guidelines to varying degrees. Of these, 124 days also exceeded Kazakhstan’s less stringent national maximum permissible concentration (MPC) of 35 µg/m³:
• 15–35 µg/m³: 93 days (25.5%). During these periods, PM2.5 concentrations exceeded WHO guidelines but formally remained within Kazakhstan’s national MPC of 35 µg/m³.
• 35–70 µg/m³ (1–2 times the MPC): 89 days (24.4%). • 70–140 µg/m³ (2–4 times the MPC): 34 days (9.3%).
• Above 140 µg/m³ (more than 4 times the MPC): 1 day. The most polluted day was December 7, when the citywide daily average PM2.5 concentration reached 145.1 µg/m³.
• In January, February, and December, virtually no days with clean air were recorded.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: • July 2025 was unusual: the number of days exceeding the WHO guideline increased to 7, compared with none in 2024. The average pollution level in July was 24% higher than in June.

One possible contributing factor was drier weather compared with the previous year. In the absence of rain and with weak winds, dust and vehicle exhaust emissions can accumulate in the air even during summer, challenging the common perception that summer air is clean.

The overall statistics confirm that air pollution in Almaty is a structural problem. For more than 60% of the year, the city experiences air pollution levels that exceed international air quality guidelines.
CHAPTER 2. The City’s Rhythms: Daily and Seasonal Patterns Daily Pollution Profiles by Season
The distribution of PM2.5 concentrations throughout the day shows a clear dependence on the season:

• Winter is the most critical season, marked by a persistently high pollution background. The average PM2.5 concentration in winter is 61.1 µg/m³, which is almost 1.8 times higher than Kazakhstan’s daily average maximum permissible concentration (MPC).
Even the average morning minimum (05:00–08:00) remains at 43–45 µg/m³, meaning concentrations exceed the national standard throughout the entire day.

Peak levels are recorded between 19:00 and 21:00 (above 80 µg/m³), which can be explained by the lowering of the planetary boundary layer (temperature inversion), combined with the evening traffic peak and peak нагрузки on autonomous heating systems.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: • Autumn shows a pattern similar to winter, but with lower amplitudes before the start of the heating season. The average PM2.5 concentration in autumn is 43 µg/m³, which also exceeds Kazakhstan’s MPC. During the daytime plateau (03:00–16:00), concentrations fluctuate around 30–40 µg/m³, hovering around the Kazakhstan MPC threshold (35 µg/m³).
The evening spike (after 16:00) causes concentrations to double by around 20:00, reaching 66–67 µg/m³.

• Spring and summer are the cleanest periods, due to better mixing of air masses and the absence of heating-related emissions. Summer is characterized by the lowest and most stable PM2.5 concentrations: the average level is 12.7 µg/m³, and for nearly 24 hours a day concentrations remain in the WHO “green zone” (below 15 µg/m³).

A slight increase is observed only around 20:00. • In spring, the pollution pattern generally mirrors summer, but with somewhat higher concentrations. The average PM2.5 concentration in spring is 18.6 µg/m³, and daily levels typically range between 15 and 25 µg/m³. The evening peak remains, reaching around 26 µg/m³, but its amplitude is significantly lower than in autumn and winter.
Impact of the Heating Season: October 10 as the Turning Point
A comparison of data before and after the official start of the heating season (based on the AirGradient sensor network) revealed a systemic transformation in air quality across the city.
To clearly illustrate these changes, the map shows the locations of AirGradient stations in Almaty and nearby settlements in Almaty Region.

The center of each marker represents air quality before the heating season (from September 1 to October 10), while the outer ring shows conditions after the start of the heating season (from October 10 to December 31). The size of each marker is proportional to the average daily concentration (from smaller to larger).

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: • Systemic Shift: Almost no monitoring locations on the city map retained a uniform color. The widespread appearance of bright red and purple rings around green and yellow centers indicates a sharp increase in PM2.5 concentrations following the start of the heating season.

• Geographic Patterns: The most pronounced differences (wide, contrasting rings) are observed in the northern and northwestern parts of the city. These are areas where emissions from individual household heating systems combine with the background impact of CHP-2 and CHP-3, creating zones of extreme environmental risk.

• Relatively Stable Areas: Only the foothill districts (the upper parts of Medeu and Bostandyk Districts) maintained relative stability, where evening mountain breezes partially offset the increase in emissions.

District-Level Analysis A quantitative analysis across Almaty’s districts confirms the patterns shown on the map. The transition to the heating season led to increased air pollution in every district without exception, particularly in the northern part of the city. However, the magnitude of this increase varied considerably.

In the city’s lower-lying districts (Alatau, Turksib, and Zhetysu), a severalfold increase in toxic pollution exposure was recorded. Following the start of the heating season on October 10, daily average PM2.
5 concentrations in these areas consistently remained within the range considered harmful to health (70–140 µg/m³), exceeding the WHO daily guideline (15 µg/m³) by 4–9 times.

Chapter 3. Geography of Air Pollution: Spatial Analysis The clearest pattern emerges when moving from the foothill districts toward the lower-lying parts of the city. The map showing the spatial distribution of average PM2.5 concentrations in October–November 2025 reveals pronounced variations in air pollution levels across Almaty, driven by both natural geographic conditions and human activities.

Southern Zone (Foothills): This area has the most favorable air quality conditions. The elevated terrain and mountain breezes provide effective air circulation, which, combined with the absence of major industrial facilities and heating plants, helps keep pollutant concentrations relatively low.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: As we move toward the central and northern districts, pollutant concentrations increase steadily. Central Almaty forms a zone of moderate pollution, reflecting high traffic density, densely built-up residential areas, and intensive urban activity.
The most unfavorable conditions are recorded in the northern and northwestern districts, where the highest concentration of monitoring locations with elevated average PM2.5 levels is observed.

The critical situation in these districts is driven not only by local emission sources (private households and industrial facilities) but also by the specific atmospheric dynamics of the Almaty Basin.
During evening and nighttime hours, a distinctive meteorological pattern develops:

• Mountain–Valley Circulation: Cooled air from the mountains (nighttime mountain breeze) moves from south to north, effectively pushing pollutants accumulated during the day from the upper and central parts of the city into lower-lying areas.

• Atmospheric Trapping: As this airflow reaches the central part of the city, it slows down. Due to limited ventilation and temperature inversions, harmful pollutants become trapped in the near-surface atmospheric layer.

• Cumulative Effect: Intensive nighttime emissions from local households add to the smog transported from the city center. As a result, PM2.5 concentrations in northern districts not only fail to decrease at night but continue to rise, creating areas of persistent pollution exposure.

During autumn and winter, pollutants accumulate in the near-surface atmospheric layer and disperse very slowly, resulting in consistently high concentrations even in the absence of extreme emission events.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: The clustering map of daily average PM2.5 concentrations confirms this pattern. Two distinct spatial clusters can be clearly identified across the city, differing in both pollution levels and geographic location. The boundary between these clusters largely follows the city’s natural slope from south to north.

The most polluted cluster (red markers) is predominantly concentrated in the northern and northwestern parts of the city, below Raimbek Avenue, including Turksib, Alatau, and Zhetysu Districts. This cluster is characterized by consistently high daily average PM2.5 concentrations, with an average sensor reading of 65.
3 µg/m³, almost twice the level recorded in the relatively cleaner cluster.

The relatively cleaner areas (green markers) are located in the southern foothill zone of the city, above Al-Farabi Avenue, including Bostandyk and Medeu Districts. These areas have significantly lower pollution levels, with average daily PM2.5 concentrations of 32.3 µg/m³.
The more favorable conditions in southern Almaty are associated with its foothill terrain, better air circulation, and a lower concentration of local emission sources.

Thus, the distribution of air pollution in Almaty is largely determined not by isolated events but by the city’s terrain, urban development patterns, and airflow dynamics. The map confirms that air pollution in Almaty has a pronounced spatial pattern and is not evenly distributed across the city.
The difference between southern and northern districts persists even when data are averaged over several months, indicating structural causes of pollution rather than isolated episodes.
District Ranking by PM2.5 Concentrations Quantitative data confirm that the pollution gap between the city’s upper and lower areas is approximately twofold.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Relatively Lower Pollution Levels: • Bostandyk District: 22.1 µg/m³ (the lowest concentration in the city)
• Auezov / Medeu Districts: 25.8 µg/m³ • Nauryzbay District: 27.1 µg/m³
Higher-Risk Areas: • Turksib District: 46.8 µg/m³ • Zhetysu District: 37.9 µg/m³
• Alatau District: 37.7 µg/m³ • Almaly District: 30.9 µg/m³ The heatmap below provides a detailed view of how the pollution burden was distributed across Almaty’s districts throughout 2025.

The figure clearly shows that Turksib, Zhetysu, and Alatau Districts remain the areas most affected by elevated pollution concentrations throughout the year. They are the first to enter the high-pollution categories (red, purple, and burgundy segments) and the last to emerge from them.

While the city’s lower-lying districts record concentrations exceeding 140 µg/m³, the southern parts of Almaty (Bostandyk and Medeu Districts) often remain within the red or even yellow categories on the same days.
The terrain and proximity to the mountains provide southern Almaty with brief periods of improved air quality that are virtually absent in the northern part of the city.
Chapter 4. Extreme Pollution Days The Cleanest and Most Polluted Days of 2025

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Throughout 2025, Almaty experienced an unprecedented difference between its minimum and maximum daily average PM2.5 concentrations, with a 29-fold variation. This clearly demonstrates how strongly air quality depends on seasonal factors, meteorological conditions, and human activities.

Top 10 Cleanest Days: The day with the most favorable air quality was October 1, 2025. On that day, the daily average PM2.5 concentration was 5.0 µg/m³, meeting even the strictest WHO annual average guideline.

However, the analysis shows that this did not represent the city’s typical background pollution level. The improvement in air quality coincided with unusual weather conditions. On October 1, Almaty experienced a sharp change in weather: nighttime temperatures ranged from +3°C to +8°C, while daytime temperatures were between +5°C and +10°C.
Wind speeds reached 9–14 m/s, with gusts of 15–29 m/s. Rainfall was also recorded, along with snowfall in mountainous areas.
Apart from October 1, the top 10 cleanest days of 2025 were predominantly in spring and summer:
• September 23 — 5.7 µg/m³ • May 26 — 6.2 µg/m³ • May 11 — 6.6 µg/m³
• July 10 — 6.7 µg/m³ • May 12 — 6.8 µg/m³ • January 23 — 7.2 µg/m³
• August 18 — 7.4 µg/m³ • July 11 — 7.7 µg/m³ • May 19 — 8.1 µg/m³

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Even on these relatively favorable days, localized exceedances were recorded in certain districts. However, they did not significantly affect the citywide average.
Top 10 Most Polluted Days: The most polluted day of the year was December 7, 2025.
December was the period of the most severe pollution burden, reaching its peak during the first ten days of the month. The daily average PM2.5 concentration reached 145.1 µg/m³.
This was 9.7 times higher than the WHO daily guideline (15 µg/m³) and 4.1 times higher than Kazakhstan’s national maximum permissible concentration (MPC) of 35 µg/m³.
At the same time, peak hourly average concentrations in certain districts reached an extreme 493 µg/m³. Such pollution levels pose a direct threat to public health.

The day was characterized by stable weather conditions with no precipitation, partly cloudy skies, and weak easterly winds (3–8 m/s). Nighttime temperatures ranged from 0°C to −2°C, while daytime temperatures reached +6°C to +8°C.
These conditions prevented pollutant dispersion, leading to their accumulation and a sharp increase in PM2.5 concentrations.

Toward the end of the day, fog and precipitation began to develop, indicating high humidity and weak vertical mixing of air masses. As a result, pollutants accumulated over the preceding hours were not dispersed, and concentrations reached extreme levels.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Overall, the top 10 most polluted days of 2025 occurred exclusively during winter:
• January 14 — 125 µg/m³ • January 15 — 121.3 µg/m³ • January 12 — 117.7 µg/m³
• February 7 — 104.9 µg/m³ • December 3 — 104.1 µg/m³ • February 9 — 104 µg/m³
• January 27 — 98.7 µg/m³ • February 8 — 97.9 µg/m³ • December 29 — 97.6 µg/m³

All these days were characterized by simultaneously elevated citywide average concentrations and extreme localized peaks, indicating a combination of increased emissions and limited pollutant dispersion.
Air Pollution by Day of the Week Extreme pollution episodes reflect the most unfavorable conditions but do not reveal regular behavioral and social patterns associated with air pollution.
An analysis of daily average PM2.5 concentrations by day of the week identified clear patterns that persist independently of isolated weather anomalies.

Sunday — The Weekly Pollution Peak: Sunday is the most polluted day of the week, with an annual average PM2.5 concentration of 37.3 µg/m³. Moreover, the highest daily average concentration of the entire year — 145.1 µg/m³ — was recorded on Sunday, December 7, indicating that some of the most severe smog episodes occur toward the end of the week.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Saturday — The Beginning of the Increase: Pollution levels begin to rise on Saturdays, reaching an average of 32.7 µg/m³, already exceeding the average concentrations recorded on weekdays.

Monday — The Lingering Weekend Effect: Monday maintains a relatively high average concentration of 31.7 µg/m³, potentially reflecting pollutants that accumulated over the weekend and had not fully dispersed by the beginning of the working week.

Wednesday and “Clean” Thursday: Pollution levels reach a local minimum in the middle of the week. Wednesday records the lowest average concentration at 27.2 µg/m³, followed closely by Thursday at 28 µg/m³, living up to its popular reputation as a relatively clean day.
The difference between the cleanest day, Wednesday, and the most polluted day, Sunday, exceeds 37%.

Tuesday and Friday: These days show moderate average concentrations of 30.4 µg/m³. However, a significant pollution spike of up to 124 µg/m³ was recorded on a Tuesday, indicating that severe but less frequent pollution episodes can also occur on weekdays.

Contrary to common expectations, weekends have higher average PM2.5 concentrations than weekdays (35.6 µg/m³ versus 29.9 µg/m³, respectively). Daily pollution patterns clearly show that this difference emerges in the evening: on weekends, concentrations rise sharply after 16:00, reaching an average peak of approximately 57 µg/m³ by 20:00.

This pattern challenges the widespread assumption that weekday traffic is the primary driver of urban smog. The data show that air quality remains consistently poor on weekends — particularly on Sundays — and sometimes deteriorates even further.

These findings suggest that attention should shift from vehicle traffic alone to a broader combination of factors. Private households burning coal and energy generation facilities likely continue to play a significant role, with heating demand remaining high or even increasing on weekends when residents spend more time at home.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Thus, the air pollution problem extends far beyond traffic congestion.

What Drives Air Pollution: Sources and Conditions Extreme air pollution levels in Almaty are not caused by isolated emissions but by a combination of continuous emission sources and weather conditions. During winter, the city regularly experiences periods of pollutant accumulation: emissions increase while conditions for their dispersion deteriorate sharply.

The beginning of the heating season marks a critical turning point in pollution levels. Data show that after October 8–10, PM2.5 concentrations rise sharply across all districts, increasing severalfold in areas dominated by private housing.
This indicates a substantial contribution from individual household heating systems and solid-fuel combustion, particularly during evening and nighttime hours.

Summer pollution differs in nature from winter smog. During warmer months, the main contributors include dust (including road and construction dust), vehicle emissions, and secondary pollutants formed under hot and sunny conditions.
In the absence of rainfall and with weak winds, particles are not removed from the atmosphere and continue to accumulate, even without heating-related emissions.
We examined motor vehicles as a source of air pollution in greater detail in a separate study, available here.
Therefore, summer does not guarantee clean air: during dry and windless weather, pollution levels may remain elevated even in the warmest months.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: Transport contributes consistently to background pollution throughout the year, particularly during evening rush hours. However, transport alone cannot explain extreme pollution levels. Its contribution becomes especially critical when atmospheric conditions limit pollutant dispersion.

In the northern and northwestern districts, emissions from major heat generation facilities combine with those from private households. During temperature inversions, this results in persistently high concentrations even at night, when traffic volumes decrease.

Differences between districts are determined not only by emission sources but also by terrain. Nighttime mountain–valley air circulation transports pollutants from the upper and central parts of the city toward lower-lying areas, where they accumulate and combine with local emissions.
This makes the northern districts areas of chronic environmental exposure.

Conclusions Analysis of the 2025 data shows that air quality in Almaty remains persistently poor and poses systemic risks to public health, with pronounced seasonal and geographic disparities. The annual average PM2.5 concentration exceeds the WHO guideline by more than six times, while the number of days with safe air quality continues to decline.

For more than half the year (217 days), Almaty residents were exposed to pollution levels exceeding international air quality guidelines. During winter, episodes of extreme pollution posed a direct threat to the health of the city’s entire population.

A defining feature of 2025 was the substantial variation in pollutant concentrations, ranging from levels close to WHO guidelines to values exceeding Kazakhstan’s maximum permissible concentration by more than four times.
This demonstrates the strong dependence of air quality on meteorological conditions, the heating season, and local emission sources.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: At the same time, the expansion of the monitoring network during the second half of the year made it possible to capture the true extent of pollution more comprehensively, particularly in districts that had previously been underrepresented in monitoring coverage.

Spatial analysis highlights the systemic nature of the problem: the most unfavorable conditions are consistently observed in the northern part of the city, while foothill districts generally experience relatively better air quality but still fail to meet long-term WHO guidelines.
During winter temperature inversions, pollution spreads across the entire city, reducing geographic differences and increasing the overall risk to public health.
Taken together, the PM2.5 concentration data demonstrate that air pollution in Almaty is a structural rather than episodic problem.

Achieving sustained improvements requires systemic measures, including reducing emissions from heat generation during the heating season, cutting transport-related emissions, prioritizing gasification and modernization of heating infrastructure, and further developing and institutionalizing independent air quality monitoring.
Appendix: Methodology and Notes This section provides technical details on data collection and explanations of the calculations used in the report.

1. Data Sources and Comparability of Periods • 2024 vs. 2025 Comparison: To ensure methodological consistency, the comparison with the previous year (in Chapter 1) covers January–September. During this period, a stable network of Clarity sensors was in operation.

• Expansion of Monitoring Coverage: Starting in October 2025, additional data sources (AirGradient, IQAir, OpenAQ, and Airkaz) were integrated into the analysis. This significantly improved data representativeness and reduced the underrepresentation of localized pollution hotspots.

chunks.title: What Was Air Quality Like in Almaty in 2025?
blocks: However, it also made direct comparisons between the fourth quarter of 2025 and earlier periods less reliable.
2. Defining the Heating Season For the analysis in Chapter 2, October 10, 2025, was selected as the reference date. This choice was based on two factors:
• Official Start: In 2025, due to an early drop in temperatures, the phased connection of buildings to district heating networks began on October 8–11.

• Response from Private Households: Monitoring data recorded a sharp, widespread increase in PM2.5 concentrations during the second ten-day period of October, confirming the beginning of active solid-fuel combustion in residential areas, independently of centralized heating schedules.
3. Monitoring Parameters • Geographic Scope: The analysis is limited to the administrative boundaries of Almaty.
• Pollutant: PM2.5 (fine particulate matter with a diameter of ≤2.5 µm).
• Data Aggregation: Data are presented as daily and monthly average concentrations.

• Units of Measurement: All values are expressed in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). This is a physical measure of particulate mass concentration and is not equivalent to the Air Quality Index (AQI) displayed on some air quality monitoring platforms.

blocks: 4. Standards and Risk Classification The following reference values were used:
• WHO Guidelines: 15 µg/m³ (daily average) and 5 µg/m³ (annual average).
• Kazakhstan’s Maximum Permissible Concentration (MPC): 35 µg/m³ (daily average).

Air Quality Risk Classification (2025): The report uses an updated classification system that allows for a more detailed assessment of health risks for Almaty residents based on the extent to which pollutant concentrations exceed both national standards and WHO guidelines.
• 🟢 0–15 µg/m³: Air is considered clean and fully complies with current WHO daily guidelines.
• 🟡 15–35 µg/m³: Concentrations exceed WHO guidelines but remain within Kazakhstan’s maximum permissible concentration (MPC).
• 🔴 35–70 µg/m³: Concentrations exceed Kazakhstan’s MPC by up to two times.
• 🟣 70–140 µg/m³: Concentrations exceed Kazakhstan’s MPC by two to four times, posing health risks to the entire population during prolonged outdoor exposure.

chunks.title: Main Sources of PM2.5 Pollution in Almaty
blocks: Analysis of an Academic Article Using PMF and HYSPLIT Methods

Research Objective The study addresses the question of which types of sources contribute to PM2.5 concentrations in Almaty and their relative contribution to pollution. It is one of the first studies in Almaty to use PMF to determine the source contribution distributions based on the chemical composition of PM2.5.
Methodology Input data and study period. The study used a year-long series of PM2.5 samples collected from August 2022 to July 2023, with chemical analysis.
Location. Sampling was conducted at a single site in Almaty (the KazNU campus).
Source apportionment. The main method was Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF), which identified five source factors.

Assessment of the spatial context. HYSPLIT was used to assess the role of particle transport by calculating 72-hour backward trajectories of air masses. The Conditional Probability Function (CPF) was also used to relate source contributions to wind direction and speed.
Main finding: five PM2.5 sources and their contributions in Almaty
The PMF analysis produced the following distribution of contributions to PM2.5 in Almaty:

chunks.title: Main Sources of PM2.5 Pollution in Almaty
blocks: 1) Urban road dust (32%) This source is associated with elevated concentrations of elements linked to brake, tire and road surface wear. These particles originate from the city’s two major highways: Al-Farabi Avenue and the Eastern Bypass Road.
Almaty is characterized by slow-moving air masses, indicating the importance of road dust resuspension under conditions of weak winds and limited dispersion.

2) Urban atmosphere (20%) The urban atmosphere factor is characterized as mixed background pollution, comprising industrial and combustion emissions, as well as the accumulation of pollutants under unfavorable ventilation conditions. Its chemical profile shows evidence of multiple source types mixing, including combinations of different elements and markers.
The accumulation of particles attributed to this factor is explained by Almaty’s geography, which limits vertical and horizontal dispersion, and by the contribution of secondary aerosols.

3) CHP plants and boiler houses (18%) The CHP plant factor is supported by the characteristics of local coal ash and the typical elemental composition associated with high-temperature coal combustion. The analysis indicates probable source directions, which the authors associate with the locations of major heat supply facilities, including CHP-2 and CHP-3.

4) Residential heating (16%) The residential heating factor includes markers associated with solid fuel combustion, transboundary emissions and the secondary formation of fine particles, as well as evidence of biomass burning and possible waste burning.

For context, the authors provide an estimate of household fuel use in Almaty, noting that gas is the predominant primary fuel. However, even a small proportion of households using solid fuels may have a significant impact when dispersion is poor during the cold season.
The possible influence of particle transport and aged air masses is also noted and supported by trajectory analysis.

chunks.title: Main Sources of PM2.5 Pollution in Almaty
blocks: 5) Vehicle exhaust (14%) This factor is characterized by elements typical of traffic-related impacts, together with elements consistent with the use of deicing materials in winter.
In their analysis, the authors associate the probable directions of these particles with areas of heavy traffic near major highways.

The Urban atmosphere and Residential heating factors contain characteristic markers of coal and biomass combustion, while the CHP plant contribution shows evidence of high-temperature coal combustion, consistent with the findings of a similar analysis for Dushanbe.

Study Limitations • Spatial representativeness. The results were obtained at a single sampling site. The authors state that the findings reflect urban trends, but interpretation must account for the local nature of the observations and the possibility that source contributions vary across city districts.
• Uncertainty in the CPF analysis. Spatial uncertainty may arise because the sampling site and the location of the meteorological data used for wind analysis do not coincide.
Implications for urban policy and recommendations for effective air quality management

1) CHP plants and major heat sources • Reducing CHP plant emissions by switching to natural gas should be prioritized. This is considered a key direction because it reduces emissions and improves heat supply efficiency, but requires infrastructure incentives and the development of public–private partnership mechanisms.
• Emission control technologies must be introduced, such as fabric filters, electrostatic precipitators, and wet desulfurization units. Currently, modern emission control methods are not being used.

chunks.title: Main Sources of PM2.5 Pollution in Almaty
blocks: • The limitations of these solutions must be considered: high installation and maintenance costs, space requirements and technical operating conditions, which are particularly critical for aging equipment.

• CHP plant modernization is identified as an urgent priority, with an emphasis on commissioning new gas-fired capacity and upgrading existing units. The EU case shows reductions of 92% in SO2 emissions, 90% in PM emissions and 70% in NOx emissions.

2) Coal and biomass combustion in the residential sector • Coal and biomass combustion in the residential sector is also identified as a top priority. International experience shows that restrictions on solid fuel combustion can significantly improve air quality.
• The main barriers are the availability of alternatives, public acceptance of the measures and low awareness of the risks, making a comprehensive package of measures necessary.
• The core measures include banning solid fuel sales, promoting cleaner fuels, providing financial support to households and systematically informing the public.
• The role of housing energy efficiency measures is emphasized, including low-cost solutions to reduce heat loss, as these reduce fuel demand and facilitate the transition to cleaner sources.
• The potential for reducing PM2.5 emissions by phasing out coal in Kazakhstan’s residential sector is 92%.
• Switching households from solid fuels to cleaner alternatives generally requires active government involvement, including subsidies and the removal of infrastructure constraints.

chunks.title: Main Sources of PM2.5 Pollution in Almaty
blocks: 3) Transport and vehicle fleet emissions • Reducing transport emissions requires the simultaneous development of public transport infrastructure, stronger enforcement of vehicle inspections and the creation of a convenient pedestrian environment.
• Reallocating street space in favor of public transport and supporting micromobility reduce air pollution.
• Transparent and regular vehicle inspections, together with differentiated charges, encourage the use of cleaner vehicles and proper maintenance, thereby reducing pollution by 12–13% in the EU.
4) Air quality management • In the absence of annual pollutant standards, achievable interim annual PM2.5 targets are proposed: 25 µg/m³ for Almaty.

• These targets could be established as Environmental Quality Standards through amendments to the Environmental Code, with subsequent revision as emission control technologies improve and monitoring data accumulate.

• For major Category I sources, including CHP plants, it is essential to strengthen enforcement, apply best available techniques (BAT) and introduce payments and fees that encourage emission reductions.

• A major limitation of the current system is insufficient monitoring infrastructure. Without it, source identification, forecasting, early warning, emission inventory development and assessment of the effectiveness of measures are difficult.
• A comprehensive strategy should include regular communication of health risks, standardized alert protocols and transparent communication during periods of elevated pollution.

chunks.title: Main Sources of PM2.5 Pollution in Almaty
blocks: Key conclusions • PM2.5 in Almaty originates from several major sources simultaneously. The PMF analysis identified five factors that account for the main contributions to particle concentrations.
• The largest contribution comes from urban road dust (32%), highlighting the importance of dust resuspension and road-related processes alongside fuel-related sources.

• A substantial share comes from coal combustion at CHP plants and in the residential sector: CHP plants and boiler houses account for an estimated 18%, and residential heating for 16%. Meanwhile, the chemical profile of the urban atmosphere factor (20%) clearly contains coal and biomass markers.

• The urban atmosphere factor (20%) reflects the accumulation and mixing of pollutants, explained by limited dispersion due to geography and meteorological conditions, as well as the contribution of secondary aerosols.
• The directions from which vehicle exhaust emissions (14%) arrive are associated with areas of heavy traffic and proximity to major highways.

• Seasonality in Almaty is driven not only by increased emissions but also by poor dispersion, so even sources with relatively small shares may have a noticeable impact during periods of unfavorable ventilation.

• The authors’ recommendations focus on four main areas of management: accelerated CHP plant modernization and conversion to gas; a package of residential heating measures with social support; public transport and vehicle inspection measures; and formalized targets supported by stronger monitoring and enforcement.
Private sector Vehicle

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: What Kazhydromet’s Data Leaves Out
blocks: The 2025 Paradox: What Kazhydromet’s Data Leaves Out Almaty Air Initiative analyzed Kazhydromet’s official reports and the publicly available raw data from its automated air quality monitoring stations for 2025.
The analysis reveals a contradictory picture of air quality in Almaty in 2025.
Key Findings from the Annual Report • Average annual pollution levels decreased by 31%. The Air Pollution Index (API) fell from 5.8 to 4.0, formally placing the city in the “low pollution” category.

• Extreme pollution episodes became more severe. The Standard Index (SI) increased from 7.9 to 9.6 (+21.5%). This means that, during one episode, the highest recorded concentration of a pollutant exceeded its maximum permissible concentration by a factor of approximately 10.
• The annual Maximum Frequency Index (MFI) increased. The index rose from 21% to 28% (+7 percentage points).

• The number of exceedances of maximum permissible concentrations changed significantly. Exceedances of the maximum one-time permissible concentration for ozone fell by approximately 100 times (−99%). Meanwhile, nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) exceedances increased to 12,309 cases (+11.6%), and nitric oxide (NO) exceedances rose to 2,749 cases (+50.2%).
The citywide annual average concentrations calculated from the raw data of automated monitoring stations, excluding manual monitoring posts, were*:
• PM2.5: 14.27 µg/m³ • PM10: 23.7 µg/m³ • SO₂: 25.0 µg/m³ • CO: 484.4 µg/m³

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: What Kazhydromet’s Data Leaves Out
blocks: • NO₂: 39.8 µg/m³ • NO: 32.7 µg/m³ • O₃: 4.9 µg/m³ Measurements vary by tens of times between stations. According to automated monitoring data, annual average PM2.5 concentrations at individual stations range from less than 1 µg/m³ to 43.6 µg/m³. This calls for a careful examination of the monitoring network’s structure.

The year was warmer and considerably drier than 2024. In some months, precipitation was several times below normal, while weather conditions were frequently dominated by anticyclonic periods with weak winds.
Such conditions limit the mixing of air masses and reduce the atmosphere’s natural cleansing processes, contributing to the accumulation of pollutants near the ground.
The 2025 Paradox: Lower Background Levels, Higher Peaks According to official data, Almaty’s air became “cleaner” in 2025. However, a more detailed analysis reveals a more complex picture.
Comparison of the SI, MFI, and API in Almaty, 2021–2025 Source: “Environmental Bulletin on the State of the Environment in Almaty City, Almaty Region, and Zhetysu Region, 2025.”
Kazhydromet uses the Air Pollution Index (API) to assess overall background pollution. Additional indicators are used to provide a more complete picture:
• SI (Standard Index) reflects the most severe pollution episode and indicates how many times the maximum concentration exceeded the established limit.
• MFI (Maximum Frequency Index) indicates how frequently pollutant concentrations exceeded permissible levels. The report uses the MFI calculated for a single monitoring station.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: What Kazhydromet’s Data Leaves Out
blocks: According to the agency’s annual report, average background pollution in Almaty decreased by 31% in 2025 compared with 2024 (API: 5.8 → 4.1), formally placing the city in the low-pollution category under the API scale.

At the same time, the report records substantial decreases across several indicators. The number of registered exceedances of maximum one-time permissible concentrations fell by 99% for ozone (from 8,036 to 77 episodes), by 79.6% for carbon monoxide (CO; from 4,406 to 898), by 34% for PM2.
5 (from 3,236 to 2,131), by 29% for PM10 (from 1,091 to 772), and by 25% for sulfur dioxide (from 2,271 to 1,704).
For reference: API (Air Pollution Index) is an indicator reflecting average annual pollution levels across a group of priority pollutants.
SI (Standard Index) represents the most extreme single pollutant concentration recorded during the year.
MFI (Maximum Frequency Index) indicates how frequently pollutant concentrations exceed sanitary limits at an individual monitoring station.

At first glance, these figures suggest an overall improvement in air quality. However, the composition of pollution has changed considerably. While ozone was among the leading pollutants in terms of exceedances in 2024 (8,036 cases), its contribution had almost disappeared by 2025 (77 cases).

At the same time, nitrogen compounds became more prominent: nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) exceedances increased from 11,024 to 12,309 cases (+11.6%), while nitric oxide (NO) exceedances rose from 1,830 to 2,749 (+50.2%). However, comparing these figures with the raw data reveals certain discrepancies.

chunks.title: The 2025 Paradox: What Kazhydromet’s Data Leaves Out
blocks: Comparison of the Number of Maximum One-Time Permissible Concentration Exceedances for Major Pollutants, According to Kazhydromet (2024–2025)
